Abstract:
Metal three-dimensional (3D) printing includes a vast number of operation and material parameters with complex dependencies, which significantly complicates process optimization, materials development, and real-time monitoring and control. We leverage ultrahigh-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging and high-fidelity multiphysics modeling to identify simple yet universal scaling laws for keyhole stability and porosity in metal 3D printing. The laws apply broadly and remain accurate for different materials, processing conditions, and printing machines. We define a dimensionless number, the Keyhole number, to predict aspect ratio of a keyhole and the morphological transition from stable at low Keyhole number to chaotic at high Keyhole number. Furthermore, we discover inherent correlation between keyhole stability and porosity formation in metal 3D printing. By reducing the dimensions of the formulation of these challenging problems, the compact scaling laws will aid process optimization and defect elimination during metal 3D printing, and potentially lead to a quantitative predictive framework. Identifying scaling laws in metal 3D printing is key to process optimization and materials development. Here the authors report scaling laws to quantify correlation between process parameters, keyhole stability and pore formation by high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging and multiphysics modeling.

In the metal additive manufacturing (AM) process of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), there are a limited number of materials suitable for producing parts with high density and desired mechanical properties. To establish novel materials, it is essential to determine optimized process parameters in order to overcome process-related challenges and mitigate defects such as lack of fusion, keyholing, and balling. Scaling laws based on thermophysical properties and process parameters can be used to transfer knowledge from other materials or LPBF systems. In this work, a scaling law is used to adjust process parameters for single-track experiments over a wide range, which are laser power P _L (100–1000 W), scan speed v _s (300–2500 mm/s), and laser spot size d _s (0.08–0.25 mm). Compared to existing studies, the parameter range is thus extended towards large laser spot sizes and high laser powers. The scaling law used is based on the calculation of the normalized enthalpy $$\frac{\Delta H}{{h}_{s}}$$ Δ H h s . The ratio of the deposited energy density $$\Delta$$ Δ H and the melting enthalpy h _s correlates with the dimensions of the melt pool. According to the aspect ratio $${\delta }_{\mathrm{c}}$$ δ c of the melt pool of each single track, the respective melting mode—conduction, transition, and keyhole mode—was identified. The process parameters of the single tracks in transition mode were used to optimize the density of the LPBF specimens with varying hatch distance h _d (0.06–0.12 mm), resulting in specimens with a relative density of > 99.8%. The proposed methodology can accelerate the process parameter finding for new alloys and avoid process-related defects. Graphical Abstract

Abstract:
Challenge 3 of the 2022 NIST additive manufacturing benchmark (AM Bench) experiments asked modelers to submit predictions for solid cooling rate, liquid cooling rate, time above melt, and melt pool geometry for single and multiple track laser powder bed fusion process using moving lasers. An in-house developed A dditive M anufacturing C omputational F luid D ynamics code (AM-CFD) combined with a cylindrical heat source is implemented to accurately predict these experiments. Heuristic heat source calibration is proposed relating volumetric energy density (ψ) based on experiments available in the literature. The parameters of the heat source of the computational model are initially calibrated based on a Higher Order Proper Generalized Decomposition- (HOPGD) based surrogate model. The prediction using the calibrated heat source agrees quantitatively with NIST measurements for different process conditions (laser spot diameter, laser power, and scan speed). A scaling law based on keyhole formation is also utilized in calibrating the parameters of the cylindrical heat source and predicting the challenge experiments. In addition, an improvement on the heat source model is proposed to relate the Volumetric Energy Density (VED_σ) to the melt pool aspect ratio. The model shows further improvement in the prediction of the experimental measurements for the melt pool, including cases at higher VED_σ. Overall, it is concluded that the appropriate selection of laser heat source parameterization scheme along with the heat source model is crucial in the accurate prediction of melt pool geometry and thermal measurements while bypassing the expensive computational simulations that consider increased physics equations.

Abstract:
A Finite element model is developed with a commercial code to investigate the keyhole dynamics and stability at keyhole threshold, a fusion regime characteristic to laser microwelding or to Laser Powder Bed Fusion. The model includes relevant physics to treat the hydrodynamic problems—surface tension, Marangoni stress, and recoil pressure—as well as a self-consistent ray-tracing algorithm to account for the “beam-trapping” effect. Implemented in both static and scanning laser configurations, the model successfully reproduces some key features that most recent x-ray images have exhibited. The dynamics of the liquid/gas interface is analyzed, in line with the distribution of the absorbed intensity as well as with the increase of the keyhole energy coupling. Based on these results, new elements are provided to discuss our current understanding of the keyhole formation and stability at threshold.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Multi-objective Bayesian Optimization (MOBO) has become a promising strategy for accelerating process development in Laser Powder Bed Fusion of Metals (PBF-LB/M), where experimental evaluations are costly, and design spaces are high-dimensional. This study investigates how different initialization strategies affect MOBO performance in a discrete, machine-limited parameter space during the fabrication of AZ31 magnesium alloy. Three approaches to constructing the initial experimental dataset—Latin Hypercube Sampling (V1), balanced-marginal selection (V2), and prior fractional-factorial sampling (V3)—were compared using two state-of-the-art MOBO algorithms, DGEMO and TSEMO, implemented within the AutoOED platform. A total of 180 samples were produced and evaluated with respect to two conflicting objectives: maximizing relative density and build rate. The evolution of the Pareto front and hypervolume metrics shows that the structure of the initial dataset strongly governs subsequent optimization efficiency. Variant V3 yielded the highest hypervolumes for both algorithms, whereas Variant V2 produced the most uniform Pareto approximation, highlighting a trade-off between global coverage and structural distribution. TSEMO demonstrated faster early convergence, whereas DGEMO maintained broader exploration of the design space. Analysis of duplicate experimental points revealed that discretization and batch selection can considerably limit the effective search diversity, contributing to an early saturation of hypervolume gains. The results indicate that, in constrained PBF-LB/M design spaces, MOBO primarily serves to validate and refine a well-designed initial dataset rather than to discover dramatically new optima. The presented workflow highlights how initialization, parameter discretization, and sampling diversity shape the practical efficiency of MOBO for additive manufacturing process optimization.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Open-loop control of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) additive manufacturing (AM) has enabled the production of complex, high-criticality parts for various industries. This method relies on static parameter sets from extensive experimentation and simulations, hoping they remain stable and defect-free in production. Closed-loop control of LPBF can further enhance process stability and reduce defects despite complex thermal histories, process noise, hardware drift, and unexpected perturbations. Controller performance depends on parameter tuning, traditionally a manual, expertise-driven process with no guarantee of optimal performance and limited transferability between systems. This study proposes Bayesian Optimization (BO) to automate in-layer controller tuning by leveraging LPBF's layer-to-layer repetitive nature. Two approaches are introduced: online tuning, adjusting parameters iteratively during the process, and offline tuning, conducted in a setup such as laser exposures on a bare metal plate. These methods are experimentally implemented on an in-layer PI controller, and the performance is investigated on two wedge geometries prone to overheating. Results show that BO effectively tunes controllers using either method, significantly reducing overheating in controlled wedge specimens compared to uncontrolled ones. This study presents the first printed parts controlled by an in-layer controller subjected to microstructural analysis. Findings reveal partial presence of lack-of-fusion porosities due to insufficient laser power assigned by the controller, highlighting a significant challenge for utilizing laser power controllers. In summary, BO presents a promising method for automatic in-layer controller tuning in LPBF, enhancing control precision and mitigating overheating in production parts.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11837-024-06946-z, doi:10.1007/s11837-024-06946-z. This article has 43 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt evaluates volumetric energy density (VED) as a predictor of defects in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) 316L stainless steel. Nine parameter sets varied laser power, scanning velocity, and hatch spacing while maintaining the same VED. Despite identical VED values, the specimens showed systematic differences in both pore type and pore amount, indicating that VED alone is only correlational and cannot represent the distinct mechanisms producing defects. The article considers keyhole porosity, lack-of-fusion (LOF) porosity, and spatter-related defects. Keyholing occurs when the laser sufficiently vaporizes material, potentially creating cavities, while LOF results from inadequate remelting or overlap between melt pools and layers. Spatter, often associated with high laser power, can land on solidifying material and generate intrapass LOF; the excerpt notes that no analytical model previously predicted when spatter or powder ejection would occur. The authors use analytical defect maps and propose a modified interpass LOF criterion plus a new spatter-induced intrapass LOF criterion, intended to improve predictions at low-power/low-speed and high-power/high-speed conditions, respectively. This excerpt does not provide numerical accuracy results or identify whether the experiments used a Concept Laser M2 system.

Smith et al. evaluated analytical defect-map models for keyhole porosity, lack-of-fusion (LOF), and newly proposed spatter-induced porosity in laser powder bed fusion of 316L stainless steel. Nine parameter combinations were examined, varying laser power, scan velocity, and hatch spacing while maintaining the same volumetric energy density. The results show that volumetric energy density alone does not reliably predict either porosity type or porosity amount: substantially different levels of LOF, gas, and spatter-induced porosity occurred at constant volumetric energy density. The study also emphasizes that defect formation depends on the combined effects of laser power, velocity, layer height, hatch spacing, and preheat temperature. Interpass LOF caused by insufficient melt-track overlap occurred at low laser powers and scan speeds and was not captured well by conventional LOF criteria based on semicircular melt-pool assumptions. A modified LOF criterion incorporating actual melt-pool width and depth geometry better predicted this porosity. At higher laser powers and scan speeds, intrapass spatter-induced LOF was associated with increased laser shock pressure. The authors conclude that defect maps organized by individual defect mechanisms provide more accurate process guidance than volumetric-energy-density relationships. The excerpt does not identify the machine as a Concept Laser M2.

Keyholing is linked to excessive heat input: laser heating can generate vapor or plasma, producing a cavity that may collapse or remain as a pore after solidification. However, keyhole formation does not necessarily mean retained porosity. The analytical keyhole criterion is based on Hann’s normalized-enthalpy concept, in which keyholing becomes more likely when normalized enthalpy exceeds a boiling-temperature-to-melting-temperature ratio. Defect maps use analytical expressions to identify laser-power and scanning-speed combinations that avoid keyhole and LOF porosity for fixed layer thickness and hatch spacing. Pawlak (2025) investigates multi-objective Bayesian optimization for PBF-LB/M processing of AZ31 magnesium alloy using three initialization variants and two MOBO algorithms. Each initial design contains 20 samples. V1 is generated without preliminary data using AutoOED and Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS); V2 selects a near-uniform subset from the discrete design space by balancing marginal parameter distributions; and V3 uses data from a three-level fractional-factorial/orthogonal-array design covering the same process-variable ranges. The process variables are laser power, point distance, laser exposure time, and hatch distance, with the experimentally limited ranges of 50–100 W, 50–100 µm, 20–100 µs, and 50–100 µm, respectively. Following initialization, DGEMO and TSEMO each propose batches of 10 parameter sets per MOBO iteration. The study runs for three iterations and evaluates performance using Pareto-front evolution and hypervolume relative to a fixed reference point. The excerpt reports 18 batches and 180 fabricated/analyzed samples overall, although the stated initial set of 20 samples per initialization variant is reported separately from that total.

### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Reference | Material | Keyhole criterion | LOF criterion | Balling criterion | Accuracy / validation result | Dataset size |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sheikh et al. (2023 preprint; 2024 peer-reviewed) | 316 stainless steel, NiTi compositions, IN718, Ti-6Al-4V, AF96, Ni-5Nb | Three alternatives were tested: melt-pool aspect ratio, normalized enthalpy, and Gan’s dimensionless keyhole number, with keyhole mode at $Ke>6$ | Two alternatives: penetration depth relative to layer thickness, and a hatch-spacing/melt-pool-overlap condition | Two alternatives based on melt-pool elongation and Plateau–Rayleigh instability, including an $L/W$ threshold of 2.3 | Twelve combinations were benchmarked. For 316 SS, overall accuracy ranged from 74.07% to 83.96%; the best reported combination used Eq. 3 for LOF, Eq. 8 for keyholing, and Eq. 6 for balling. The later probabilistic ensemble reported LOF accuracy as high as 87.95% for LOF1–KH3–Ball2, but that is defect-specific rather than overall accuracy. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) | 83 literature single-track observations for 316 SS; maps evaluated 12 combinations on a $20\times15$ $P$–$v$ grid at 80 µm beam diameter, 30 µm layer thickness, and 70 µm hatch spacing. (pqac-00000008) |
| Gan et al. (2021) | Multiple metals, machines, and laser-processing conditions | $Ke$ is a dimensionless function of absorbed power $\eta P$, $\rho C_p$, thermal diffusivity $\alpha$, scan speed $V_s$, spot radius $r_0$, and $T_l-T_0$. Regimes: conduction, $Ke<1.4$; transition, $1.4\le Ke\le6$; keyhole, $Ke>6$. Stable/low-defect behavior was associated with $Ke<16$, whereas chaotic keyholes and greater pore/spatter risk occurred at $Ke>30$. (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049) | Separate normalized-energy-density term captures the low-energy/LOF side; LOF diminishes around normalized energy density $\approx5$. (pqac-00000050) | Not modeled as a separate balling boundary | Synchrotron radiography and multiphysics simulations supported universal keyhole scaling. A combined porosity law using normalized energy density and a keyhole/diffusion-length parameter gave $R^2=0.92$ across independent literature datasets. Applicability is quasi-steady track interiors, not starts, stops, or turns. (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000051) | Porosity compilation from 6 independent studies and 10 process-parameter sets, plus synchrotron and simulation datasets spanning materials and machines. (pqac-00000046) |
| Smith et al. (2024) | Gas-atomized 316L on a 3D Systems DMP Flex 350; all coupons nominally at 85 J/mm³ VED | Hann-type normalized-enthalpy criterion comparing deposited enthalpy with the boiling-to-melting temperature requirement; the study stresses that keyhole formation does not guarantee retained keyhole porosity. (pqac-00000072) | Conventional geometric interpass LOF was replaced by a modified semi-elliptical overlap criterion using measured/predicted melt-pool width and depth; a separate laser-shock-pressure criterion was introduced for spatter-induced intrapass LOF. (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000070, pqac-00000071, pqac-00000073) | No principal balling boundary was validated | Nine equal-VED settings produced systematically different pore populations, disproving VED as a sufficient defect predictor. The modified interpass-LOF criterion better captured low-$P$/low-$v$ defects, while the spatter criterion addressed high-$P$/high-$v$ intrapass defects; no single numerical classification accuracy was reported in the cited passages. (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000070) | 9 combinations of power, scan speed, and hatch spacing at 85 J/mm³. (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000072) |
| Wang, Ning & Liang (2021) | Ti-6Al-4V, IN718, and 316L | Normalized-enthalpy/evaporation threshold involving absorptivity, power, speed, beam diameter, diffusivity, heat capacity, and melting/boiling temperatures | Geometric overlap condition $H^2/W^2+L^2/D^2\le1$ for adequate fusion, where $H$ is hatch spacing, $L$ layer thickness, and $W,D$ melt-pool width and depth | Capillary-stability condition based on melt-pool dimensions, reported as $\pi w/l>1$ for a stable track | Predicted thresholds were compared with published experiments and described as showing good agreement. Reported LOF thresholds were approximately 110 J/mm³ for Ti-6Al-4V and 160 J/mm³ for IN718; the cited passages do not provide a 316L-specific error metric or threshold. (pqac-00000074, pqac-00000075, pqac-00000076) | Published experimental datasets for the three alloys; exact total count was not stated in the cited passages. (pqac-00000075) |


*Table: Comparison of experimentally checked lack-of-fusion, keyhole, and balling criteria used in LPBF printability maps. It distinguishes overall classification accuracy from defect-specific validation and records the applicable dataset and processing conditions.*

{"answer": "## Calibration, Validation, and Experimental Design for LPBF Melt-Pool and Printability Models: A Literature Synthesis

### 1. Bayesian Calibration of Melt-Pool Models

The following table summarizes key Bayesian calibration campaigns for LPBF melt-pool models:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Eagar–Tsai calibration for 316L.** Whalen, Ma, and Balachandran (2021; DOI: 10.1007/s40192-021-00238-z) performed Bayesian inference on a modified Eagar–Tsai (E-T) conduction model using approximately 30 316L single-track melt-pool depth measurements combined from the Bertoli et al. and Kamath et al. datasets (layer thicknesses 30 and 50 µm). The calibrated parameters were apparent absorptivity and powder-bed porosity; beam radius was specified (average of 55 and 52 µm from the source studies) rather than inferred (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000004). The likelihood assumed 15 µm depth standard deviation for measurement variability, with weakly informative normal priors: mean absorptivity of 0.68 for SS316L, mean porosity of 0.40, both constrained to [0, 1] (pqac-00000066). MCMC was used to generate posteriors. The fitted power-dependent absorptivity was A = 0.148 ln(P) − 0.0879 (R² = 0.77) and porosity φ = 0.0015P + 0.1626 (R² = 0.96) (pqac-00000002). The principal remaining discrepancy is that conduction physics underpredicts melt-pool depth once keyholing sets in, and isolated experimental conduction-mode tracks were misclassified as keyhole (pqac-00000002). No separate Kennedy–O'Hagan model-discrepancy Gaussian process was used in that work. The calibration was also performed for Ti-6Al-4V and IN718, with analogous prior absorptivities of 0.74 and 0.67, respectively (pqac-00000066). **This is strongly supported as the primary Bayesian E-T calibration for 316L.**

**Texas A&M (TAMU) framework.** Zhang et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2021.102018) calibrated the E-T model against single-track experiments using a Kennedy–O'Hagan-style framework: a GP surrogate trained from 1,000 E-T simulations captured forward-model behavior, and a GP discrepancy function δ(x) absorbed systematic model–experiment differences (pqac-00000001). Materials included Ni-5Nb (40 single tracks; absorptivity 0.51, thermal conductivity 70.4 W/(m·K), specific heat 636.19 J/(kg·K)), NiTi (60 tracks; absorptivity 0.56), and AF9628 (absorptivity approximated from published 316L measurements) (pqac-00000079, pqac-00000082). Calibrated width and depth errors for one case were 3.6% and 4.05% MAPE, respectively (pqac-00000080). Errors increased for linear energy density below 300 J/m, requiring additional experiments in that regime (pqac-00000080, pqac-00000082). Keyholing was classified by width-to-depth thresholds: W/D ≤ 1.2 for Ni-5Nb and W/D ≤ 2 for NiTi (pqac-00000077, pqac-00000080). Experiments were on a 3D Systems ProX 200 DMP (1070 nm fiber laser, max 260 W) under argon (pqac-00000078).

**FE model calibration with GP emulator.** Fody, Leser, and Narra (2025 preprint; DOI: 10.2139/ssrn.5185945) calibrated a Goldak-inspired 3D FE thermal model for Ti-6Al-4V on an EOS M 290. Three parameters were inferred: effective absorptivity (aeff), normalized heat-source depth (Ds), and normalized heat-source radius (Rs), with uniform priors on [0.01, 100], [0.8, 100], and [0.4, 10], respectively (pqac-00000067). Data comprised 29/25/29 melt-pool cross-section images per condition at three P–v pairs. A heteroscedastic GP emulator was trained with 6 Latin-hypercube seeds plus 32 active-learning evaluations per calibration (38 total training points), and sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) generated 40,000 posterior samples (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000067). A strong identifiability challenge required imposing a maximum-temperature constraint: without it, absorptivity, radius, and depth were highly correlated, admitting a continuous range of similarly likely posteriors (pqac-00000062). With the constraint, all 29 observations fell within the 95.4% posterior-predictive contour; surrogate-to-FE validation MAPE was 0.53% (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000064). Withholding ~25% of melt-pool sections produced qualitatively similar calibrations, suggesting the data budget could potentially be reduced (pqac-00000064).

**Practical implication for the planned build.** These studies consistently show that ~25–60 single-track or cross-section melt-pool measurements per alloy or condition are sufficient for Bayesian calibration, but the remaining discrepancy is dominated by the physics absent from conduction models (Marangoni convection, vapor depression, absorptivity transitions). Measuring both melt-pool width and depth (not just one) substantially improves parameter identifiability.

---

### 2. Printability Maps: Criteria, Validation, and Accuracy

The following table compares experimentally validated printability-map criteria:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Texas A&M automated framework.** Sheikh et al. (2023 preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2304.04113; 2024 peer-reviewed, DOI: 10.1038/s41524-024-01436-x) constructed printability maps using CALPHAD-derived properties (Thermo-Calc databases including TCHEA5 and TCNI11) fed to the E-T model, with Gladush–Smurov correction for keyhole depth (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034). They evaluated 12 combinations of two LOF criteria, two balling criteria, and three keyhole criteria (pqac-00000011). For 316 stainless steel, evaluated against 83 literature single-track data points on a 20×15 P–v grid (beam diameter 80 µm, layer thickness 30 µm, hatch spacing 70 µm), the best combination achieved 83.96% overall accuracy (pqac-00000008). The highest LOF-specific accuracy was 87.95% (LOF1–KH3–Ball2) (pqac-00000009). For NiTi, the best criterion set (Eq. 4 for LOF, Eq. 6 for balling, Eq. 10 for keyhole) achieved 84–91% accuracy across three compositions (pqac-00000014). **Balling was consistently the weakest classification**, largely because experimental balling points tended to fall near boundaries with other defect regimes (pqac-00000014). The ensemble probabilistic map weights each of the 12 combinations by its accuracy using a softmax function, so that more accurate criteria contribute more strongly (pqac-00000013).

**Gan et al. Keyhole number.** Gan et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-021-22704-0) defined the dimensionless Keyhole number Ke as a function of absorbed power ηP, density ρ, heat capacity Cp, thermal diffusivity α, scan speed Vs, spot radius r0, and the liquidus-to-substrate temperature difference (Tl − T0) (pqac-00000047). The regime boundaries are: conduction mode for Ke < 1.4, transition mode for 1.4 ≤ Ke ≤ 6.0, and keyhole mode for Ke > 6.0 (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049). The normalized keyhole aspect ratio follows e* = 0.4(Ke − 1.4) (pqac-00000047). For stability: keyhole fluctuations are small and porosity is nearly absent for Ke < 16; the keyhole becomes chaotic with significant porosity and spatter risk for Ke > 30 (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000049). A porosity-volume-fraction scaling law using Ke together with normalized energy density achieved R² = 0.92 across six independent literature datasets and ten process-parameter sets (pqac-00000046). **This criterion applies to quasi-steady-state track interiors only**—not to scan starts, stops, or turning points (pqac-00000051). This is strongly supported by synchrotron X-ray imaging and high-fidelity multiphysics simulations.

**316L-specific defect criteria.** Smith et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1007/s11837-024-06946-z) demonstrated that nine parameter sets at constant VED = 85 J/mm³ on a 3D Systems DMP Flex 350 with 316L produced systematically different defect populations, definitively showing that VED alone is not a sufficient predictor (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000070). They proposed two modifications: (i) a semi-elliptical interpass LOF criterion using measured melt-pool width and depth (replacing semicircular assumptions), and (ii) a laser-shock-pressure criterion for spatter-induced intrapass LOF at high P and high v (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000073). The modified criteria better captured defects at the low-P/low-v and high-P/high-v extremes, respectively (pqac-00000070). **Weakly supported: no overall classification accuracy metric was reported in the accessible portions of that paper.**

Wang, Ning, and Liang (2021; DOI: 10.3390/app112412053) provided analytical threshold predictions for Ti-6Al-4V (LOF ~110 J/mm³), IN718 (LOF ~160 J/mm³), and 316L (properties: density 7633 kg/m³, thermal conductivity 25 W/(m·°C), specific heat 594 J/(kg·°C), absorptivity 0.35), using geometric LOF (H²/W² + L²/D² ≤ 1), capillary balling (πw/l > 1), and normalized-enthalpy keyholing criteria (pqac-00000074, pqac-00000076).

---

### 3. Experiment Design for Separating Absorptivity from Spot Size and Heat Accumulation

**Absorptivity measurements for 316L.** Trapp et al. (2017; DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2017.08.006) performed in situ calorimetric absorptivity measurements on bare polished 316L discs and ~100 µm powder-coated layers at 30–540 W and 100–1500 mm/s, using a 60 ± 5 µm Gaussian spot at 1070 nm (pqac-00000029). Key findings: bare-plate absorptivity in conduction mode was approximately 0.29–0.31; at the keyhole threshold (~70 W at 500 mm/s, or ~48 ± 10 W at 100 mm/s and ~108 ± 20 W at 1500 mm/s), absorptivity rose sharply and saturated at approximately 0.78 (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000027). Powder layers initially exhibited about 2× the bare-plate absorptivity, but this dropped sharply once the powder was fully melted; above the keyhole transition, powder and bare surfaces showed broadly similar absorptivity behavior, with saturation around 0.7–0.8 for steel (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026). This is a strongly supported, highly cited (662 citations) primary source.

**Spot size / defocus experiments.** Metelkova et al. (2018; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2018.08.006; 366 citations) systematically varied defocus on 316L at ±8 mm beyond the Rayleigh length, producing beam diameters of ~205 and ~262 µm, combined with P = 400–800 W and v = 50–250 mm/s (pqac-00000019). At constant P and v, changing defocus from +8 to −8 mm increased melt-pool depth by 204% while width changed only 22%; at lower power, the depth difference was smaller (+81%) (pqac-00000022). They reported a potential productivity increase of 840% (reaching 18.8 mm³/s) using a defocused hull-core strategy (pqac-00000017). Tenbrock et al. (2020; DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2019.116514; 179 citations) used top-hat beam profiles at 100, 150, and 200 µm spot diameters with 140–300 W in 316L LPBF, explicitly noting that larger raw beam diameters shorten the Rayleigh length, requiring careful beam characterization (pqac-00000016). Sow et al. (2020; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2020.101532; 254 citations) compared 80 µm Gaussian and 500 µm top-hat spots: the large spot produced shallow conduction-mode pools, suppressed vaporization and spatter, achieved near-zero porosity, and provided a 20–50% build-rate increase, while the 80 µm spot showed 0.3–0.5% porosity from keyhole instabilities (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

**Practical strategy for separating effects.** To deconfound absorptivity from beam size and from heat accumulation, the literature supports:  
(i) Varying defocus at fixed P and v to isolate beam-diameter effects (Metelkova 2018);  
(ii) Constant P/v lines at different speeds to separate linear energy density from interaction time and intensity;  
(iii) Bare-plate single tracks versus powder-on-plate single tracks to isolate powder effects (Trapp 2017);  
(iv) Single tracks versus multi-track walls versus cubes to isolate heat accumulation from neighboring tracks and layers (Zhang et al. 2021 used single tracks for calibration, then density coupons for validation).

---

### 4. Should a Second Spot Size Be Added to the First Build?

The literature strongly supports that spot size is a physically independent variable—not merely a secondary effect of VED—because it determines local intensity, Rayleigh length, keyhole onset threshold, and melt-pool aspect ratio independently of P and v (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). Metelkova et al. showed that in 316L LPBF, defocus alone can change melt-pool depth by over 200% at constant P and v (pqac-00000022). Normalized enthalpy ΔH/hs, which explicitly includes beam diameter, provides a more physically continuous relationship with melt-pool depth than VED across different speeds (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000022).

**Recommendation (moderately supported by synthesis of multiple studies):** The first build of 84 walls at a fixed 130 µm spot, with 60 P–v combinations spanning the full conduction-to-keyhole range, provides strong constraints on the E-T or Thermo-Calc AM model at that one spot size. However, without a second spot size, absorptivity and effective beam radius are confounded in any calibration: the same melt-pool geometry can be reproduced by trading one for the other (pqac-00000062). Given the practical constraint that the Concept Laser M2 has limited defocus control (beam quality, Rayleigh length, and actual delivered profile must be carefully characterized—pqac-00000016), **the safest strategy is to save a dedicated defocus build for the second build**, where it can be properly characterized with beam-caustic measurements and the initial E-T calibration can be used as a prior. If a small defocus experiment (e.g., 5–10 walls at a 50–80 µm or ~200 µm defocused spot) can be added to the first build without compromising the core design, this would provide early data on spot-size sensitivity. However, this requires verifying that the defocused spot profile is known and stable (pqac-00000016).

---

### 5. Batch Bayesian Optimization and Active Learning for LPBF

**McCarthy (2025 thesis, Ti-6Al-4V m-LPBF).** The initial design used a central composite design (CCD) with factorial, axial, and center points. Each subsequent active-learning iteration selected 24 unique feature vectors plus 8 center replicates from the CCD (pqac-00000038). The acquisition function was a greedy predictive-variance criterion (Zhao et al.'s weight information gain/expected model change maximization), applied to 1,000 randomly subsampled candidates per iteration (pqac-00000038). The study was constrained to three total prints/builds (one initial + two active-learning iterations) due to cost and timeline (pqac-00000038). Center replicates were analyzed with a fixed-effect one-way ANOVA to test whether batch significantly affected relative density (pqac-00000039). Non-dominated solutions from NSGA-II optimization were not experimentally validated (pqac-00000042).

**Pawlak (2025, AZ31 PBF-LB/M; DOI: 10.3390/app152412968).** A total of 180 samples were produced and evaluated for relative density and build rate (pqac-00000086). Three initialization strategies were compared: Latin Hypercube Sampling (V1), balanced-marginal selection (V2), and prior fractional-factorial sampling (V3), each with 20 initial samples (pqac-00000084). DGEMO and TSEMO algorithms then proposed batches of 10 parameter sets per MOBO iteration for three additional iterations (pqac-00000084). V3 (fractional-factorial initialization) achieved the highest hypervolume; TSEMO converged faster early while DGEMO explored more broadly (pqac-00000086, pqac-00000087). Critically, **60–80% of proposed candidates in some batches were duplicates** due to design-space discretization, limiting effective search diversity and causing early saturation of hypervolume improvement (pqac-00000090). The author noted that conventional PBF-LB/M campaigns typically investigate 10–20 parameter sets to identify a viable process window (pqac-00000086, pqac-00000058).

**Zhang, Parnell, Brabazon, and Benavoli (2021; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2107.12809).** In a binder-jetting 316L example, the initial design used a Taguchi L27 orthogonal array (27 settings, 4 replicates each), and BO selected batches of 2 new settings at a time (pqac-00000053). They reviewed acquisition functions including EI, qEI, UCB, KG, entropy search, Thompson sampling, and their batch extensions (qKG, dKG, bUCB) (pqac-00000055). One cited AM study initialized with a Latin-hypercube batch of 200 samples in 5D, followed by 35 MCMC-generated samples (pqac-00000055).

**Multi-fidelity BO (Dou 2025).** A multi-fidelity framework combining inexpensive and expensive thermal simulations used UCB acquisition for high-fidelity sampling and maximum posterior standard deviation for low-fidelity sampling, with a fixed high-to-low fidelity ratio r = m/n (typically n = 1 high-fidelity evaluation per iteration) (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000057).

---

### 6. Thermo-Calc AM Module and CALPHAD-Coupled Models

The Thermo-Calc AM Module provides CALPHAD-based thermophysical properties (liquidus, solidus, latent heat, density, thermal conductivity, heat capacity, surface tension, viscosity) and reportedly includes both steady-state and transient melt-pool calculations. The TAMU automated framework (Sheikh et al. 2023/2024) uses Thermo-Calc databases including TCHEA5, TCAL7, and TCNI11 to supply these properties, which are then fed to the E-T analytical model for melt-pool prediction and printability-map generation (pqac-00000033). Sjöström, Durga, and Lindwall (2022; DOI: 10.3389/fmats.2022.797226) linked Simufact Additive thermal simulations with Thermo-Calc microscale models (DICTRA) for 18Ni300 maraging steel, predicting micro-segregation and martensite-start temperature as functions of process parameters (pqac-00000037). Sargent et al. (2021; DOI: 10.3390/met11040570) used Thermo-Calc 2020b for CALPHAD-based non-equilibrium solidification modeling of SS316L, with material properties interpolated at 700 K: density 7.9 g/cm³, thermal conductivity 20.2 W/(m·K), and specific heat 470 J/(kg·K) (pqac-00000035).

**Important caveat:** No peer-reviewed independent validation of the Thermo-Calc AM Module's built-in printability-map predictions against experimental defect data was identified in the accessible literature. The available studies use Thermo-Calc primarily as a property provider rather than as an end-to-end validated printability tool. This is a **weakly supported gap**: the module may have been validated internally or in unpublished industrial work, but independent experimental benchmarks are lacking.

---

### 7. Recommendations for the Planned 84-Wall Build and Subsequent Bayesian-Optimization Builds

Based on the synthesized literature, the following design recommendations emerge:

**(a) First build (84 walls, 130 µm spot).** The 60 Sobol-sequence P–v combinations spanning P = 150–370 W and P/v = 0.09–0.55 J/mm (VED ~33–204 J/mm³) provide excellent coverage of the conduction-to-keyhole transition for a single spot size, consistent with the TAMU approach of 40–60 single-track experiments per alloy (pqac-00000082). The scrambled Sobol sequence is a space-filling quasi-random design well-suited for GP surrogate training. The 21 replicated pairs (walls printed in both orientations on the rotated fourth panel) serve dual purposes: quantifying recoater-direction effects and providing variance estimates essential for the likelihood in Bayesian calibration (cf. Trapp et al.'s repeated-track measurements, pqac-00000024). The control walls at the production parameter set provide anchor points for model validation.

**(b) Melt-pool observables.** Measuring both melt-pool width and depth from the etched last-layer cross-sections is critical for identifiability, as demonstrated by Fody et al.'s finding that absorptivity, depth, and radius are non-identifiable from width–depth data alone without additional constraints (pqac-00000062). Measuring porosity fraction in each wall core (the planned >0.2 mm from faces, >1 mm from base/top exclusion) provides the defect classification needed for printability-map validation.

**(c) Calibration approach.** Use the wall porosity and melt-pool boundary data to: (i) fit apparent absorptivity and powder-bed porosity in the E-T model following Whalen et al.'s MCMC approach, with weakly informative priors centered at A ≈ 0.35–0.68 for 316L (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000074); (ii) add a GP discrepancy function following Zhang et al.'s Kennedy–O'Hagan framework to capture systematic model–experiment differences (pqac-00000001); (iii) classify each wall as defect-free, LOF, keyhole, or balling to benchmark the Thermo-Calc AM Module's printability predictions and the Gan et al. Ke criterion (Ke > 6 for keyhole onset, pqac-00000047).

**(d) Second and later builds (Bayesian optimization).** The McCarthy (2025) precedent of 24 unique conditions + 8 center replicates per batch across 3 builds is a practical template (pqac-00000038). With 84 wall positions available per build, the budget is generous: consider allocating ~60 BO-selected conditions, ~15 replicates at a few key settings (for variance estimation and batch-effect testing), and ~5–9 hold-out points from the first build's well-characterized settings (for validating the BO surrogate's predictive accuracy). The Pawlak (2025) finding that duplicate proposals can reach 60–80% in discrete spaces argues for including a distance-based penalization in the acquisition function or using a continuous-relaxation strategy (pqac-00000090). The first build's 60 calibrated settings serve as an informative initialization for the GP surrogate—superior to cold-start approaches (pqac-00000087).

**(e) Second spot size.** Defer the second spot size to Build 2 or 3, once the 130 µm model is calibrated and the actual defocused beam profile can be measured with a beam-caustic diagnostic. Even 10–15 walls at a well-characterized ~200 µm defocused spot would break the absorptivity–spot-size degeneracy (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019). The normalized enthalpy ΔH/hs, which explicitly includes beam diameter, should be used rather than VED for cross-spot-size comparisons (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000022).

---

### Summary of Evidence Strength

| Statement | Support level |
|---|---|
| E-T absorptivity and porosity are Bayesian-calibratable from ~30 316L melt-pool depths | Strong (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002) |
| Kennedy–O'Hagan GP discrepancy improves E-T calibration | Moderate (pqac-00000001; demonstrated for Ni alloys, not yet specifically 316L with discrepancy GP) |
| Ke > 6 for keyhole onset, R² = 0.92 for porosity | Strong (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047; synchrotron-validated, 332 citations) |
| 316L printability map ~84% overall accuracy | Moderate (pqac-00000008; based on literature data, not single-machine validation) |
| VED is insufficient as a sole defect predictor for 316L | Strong (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000070; directly demonstrated) |
| 316L absorptivity: bare ~0.3, keyhole saturation ~0.78 | Strong (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000027; calorimetric measurements) |
| Defocus changes 316L melt-pool depth >200% at constant P,v | Strong (pqac-00000022; 366 citations) |
| Thermo-Calc AM Module independently validated for printability | Weak (no accessible peer-reviewed independent validation found) |
| Batch BO with ~20 init + 10/batch for 3–4 builds is practical | Moderate (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000084; different alloys and machines) |

### Key Open Datasets and Tables for Comparison

- **Kamath et al. (2014; DOI: 10.1007/s00170-014-5954-9):** 316L density data on a Concept Laser M2 with 54 µm spot, powers to 400 W—directly comparable to the user's machine (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000023).
- **Sheikh et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1038/s41524-024-01436-x):** Table 3 reports LOF accuracy for each criterion combination for 316 SS; Figure 5 shows predicted vs. experimental defect classifications (pqac-00000009).
- **Gan et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-021-22704-0):** Supplementary data include multi-material keyhole and porosity datasets; the keyhole scaling and porosity model could be directly evaluated against the planned 84-wall porosity measurements (pqac-00000046).
- **Trapp et al. (2017; DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2017.08.006):** Figures contain 316L absorptivity vs. power curves at 100, 500, and 1500 mm/s for both bare and powder-coated substrates (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025).
- **Pawlak (2025; DOI: 10.3390/app152412968):** Supplementary Table S1 contains all 180 AZ31 samples' process parameters and responses, useful as a MOBO benchmark (pqac-00000056)."}

{"answer": "## Calibration, Validation, and Experimental Design for LPBF Melt-Pool and Printability Models: A Literature Synthesis

### 1. Bayesian Calibration of Melt-Pool Models

The following table summarizes key Bayesian calibration campaigns for LPBF melt-pool models:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Eagar–Tsai calibration for 316L.** Whalen, Ma, and Balachandran (2021; DOI: 10.1007/s40192-021-00238-z) performed Bayesian inference on a modified Eagar–Tsai (E-T) conduction model using approximately 30 316L single-track melt-pool depth measurements combined from the Bertoli et al. and Kamath et al. datasets (layer thicknesses 30 and 50 µm). The calibrated parameters were apparent absorptivity and powder-bed porosity; beam radius was specified (average of 55 and 52 µm from the source studies) rather than inferred (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000004). The likelihood assumed 15 µm depth standard deviation for measurement variability, with weakly informative normal priors: mean absorptivity of 0.68 for SS316L, mean porosity of 0.40, both constrained to [0, 1] (pqac-00000066). MCMC was used to generate posteriors. The fitted power-dependent absorptivity was A = 0.148 ln(P) − 0.0879 (R² = 0.77) and porosity φ = 0.0015P + 0.1626 (R² = 0.96) (pqac-00000002). The principal remaining discrepancy is that conduction physics underpredicts melt-pool depth once keyholing sets in, and isolated experimental conduction-mode tracks were misclassified as keyhole (pqac-00000002). No separate Kennedy–O'Hagan model-discrepancy Gaussian process was used in that work. The calibration was also performed for Ti-6Al-4V and IN718, with analogous prior absorptivities of 0.74 and 0.67, respectively (pqac-00000066). **This is strongly supported as the primary Bayesian E-T calibration for 316L.**

**Texas A&M (TAMU) framework.** Zhang et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2021.102018) calibrated the E-T model against single-track experiments using a Kennedy–O'Hagan-style framework: a GP surrogate trained from 1,000 E-T simulations captured forward-model behavior, and a GP discrepancy function δ(x) absorbed systematic model–experiment differences (pqac-00000001). Materials included Ni-5Nb (40 single tracks; absorptivity 0.51, thermal conductivity 70.4 W/(m·K), specific heat 636.19 J/(kg·K)), NiTi (60 tracks; absorptivity 0.56), and AF9628 (absorptivity approximated from published 316L measurements) (pqac-00000079, pqac-00000082). Calibrated width and depth errors for one case were 3.6% and 4.05% MAPE, respectively (pqac-00000080). Errors increased for linear energy density below 300 J/m, requiring additional experiments in that regime (pqac-00000080, pqac-00000082). Keyholing was classified by width-to-depth thresholds: W/D ≤ 1.2 for Ni-5Nb and W/D ≤ 2 for NiTi (pqac-00000077, pqac-00000080). Experiments were on a 3D Systems ProX 200 DMP (1070 nm fiber laser, max 260 W) under argon (pqac-00000078).

**FE model calibration with GP emulator.** Fody, Leser, and Narra (2025 preprint; DOI: 10.2139/ssrn.5185945) calibrated a Goldak-inspired 3D FE thermal model for Ti-6Al-4V on an EOS M 290. Three parameters were inferred: effective absorptivity (aeff), normalized heat-source depth (Ds), and normalized heat-source radius (Rs), with uniform priors on [0.01, 100], [0.8, 100], and [0.4, 10], respectively (pqac-00000067). Data comprised 29/25/29 melt-pool cross-section images per condition at three P–v pairs. A heteroscedastic GP emulator was trained with 6 Latin-hypercube seeds plus 32 active-learning evaluations per calibration (38 total training points), and sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) generated 40,000 posterior samples (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000067). A strong identifiability challenge required imposing a maximum-temperature constraint: without it, absorptivity, radius, and depth were highly correlated, admitting a continuous range of similarly likely posteriors (pqac-00000062). With the constraint, all 29 observations fell within the 95.4% posterior-predictive contour; surrogate-to-FE validation MAPE was 0.53% (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000064). Withholding ~25% of melt-pool sections produced qualitatively similar calibrations, suggesting the data budget could potentially be reduced (pqac-00000064).

**Practical implication for the planned build.** These studies consistently show that ~25–60 single-track or cross-section melt-pool measurements per alloy or condition are sufficient for Bayesian calibration, but the remaining discrepancy is dominated by the physics absent from conduction models (Marangoni convection, vapor depression, absorptivity transitions). Measuring both melt-pool width and depth (not just one) substantially improves parameter identifiability.

---

### 2. Printability Maps: Criteria, Validation, and Accuracy

The following table compares experimentally validated printability-map criteria:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Texas A&M automated framework.** Sheikh et al. (2023 preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2304.04113; 2024 peer-reviewed, DOI: 10.1038/s41524-024-01436-x) constructed printability maps using CALPHAD-derived properties (Thermo-Calc databases including TCHEA5 and TCNI11) fed to the E-T model, with Gladush–Smurov correction for keyhole depth (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034). They evaluated 12 combinations of two LOF criteria, two balling criteria, and three keyhole criteria (pqac-00000011). For 316 stainless steel, evaluated against 83 literature single-track data points on a 20×15 P–v grid (beam diameter 80 µm, layer thickness 30 µm, hatch spacing 70 µm), the best combination achieved 83.96% overall accuracy (pqac-00000008). The highest LOF-specific accuracy was 87.95% (LOF1–KH3–Ball2) (pqac-00000009). For NiTi, the best criterion set (Eq. 4 for LOF, Eq. 6 for balling, Eq. 10 for keyhole) achieved 84–91% accuracy across three compositions (pqac-00000014). **Balling was consistently the weakest classification**, largely because experimental balling points tended to fall near boundaries with other defect regimes (pqac-00000014). The ensemble probabilistic map weights each of the 12 combinations by its accuracy using a softmax function, so that more accurate criteria contribute more strongly (pqac-00000013).

**Gan et al. Keyhole number.** Gan et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-021-22704-0) defined the dimensionless Keyhole number Ke as a function of absorbed power ηP, density ρ, heat capacity Cp, thermal diffusivity α, scan speed Vs, spot radius r0, and the liquidus-to-substrate temperature difference (Tl − T0) (pqac-00000047). The regime boundaries are: conduction mode for Ke < 1.4, transition mode for 1.4 ≤ Ke ≤ 6.0, and keyhole mode for Ke > 6.0 (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049). The normalized keyhole aspect ratio follows e* = 0.4(Ke − 1.4) (pqac-00000047). For stability: keyhole fluctuations are small and porosity is nearly absent for Ke < 16; the keyhole becomes chaotic with significant porosity and spatter risk for Ke > 30 (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000049). A porosity-volume-fraction scaling law using Ke together with normalized energy density achieved R² = 0.92 across six independent literature datasets and ten process-parameter sets (pqac-00000046). **This criterion applies to quasi-steady-state track interiors only**—not to scan starts, stops, or turning points (pqac-00000051). This is strongly supported by synchrotron X-ray imaging and high-fidelity multiphysics simulations.

**316L-specific defect criteria.** Smith et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1007/s11837-024-06946-z) demonstrated that nine parameter sets at constant VED = 85 J/mm³ on a 3D Systems DMP Flex 350 with 316L produced systematically different defect populations, definitively showing that VED alone is not a sufficient predictor (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000070). They proposed two modifications: (i) a semi-elliptical interpass LOF criterion using measured melt-pool width and depth (replacing semicircular assumptions), and (ii) a laser-shock-pressure criterion for spatter-induced intrapass LOF at high P and high v (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000073). The modified criteria better captured defects at the low-P/low-v and high-P/high-v extremes, respectively (pqac-00000070). **Weakly supported: no overall classification accuracy metric was reported in the accessible portions of that paper.**

Wang, Ning, and Liang (2021; DOI: 10.3390/app112412053) provided analytical threshold predictions for Ti-6Al-4V (LOF ~110 J/mm³), IN718 (LOF ~160 J/mm³), and 316L (properties: density 7633 kg/m³, thermal conductivity 25 W/(m·°C), specific heat 594 J/(kg·°C), absorptivity 0.35), using geometric LOF (H²/W² + L²/D² ≤ 1), capillary balling (πw/l > 1), and normalized-enthalpy keyholing criteria (pqac-00000074, pqac-00000076).

---

### 3. Experiment Design for Separating Absorptivity from Spot Size and Heat Accumulation

**Absorptivity measurements for 316L.** Trapp et al. (2017; DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2017.08.006) performed in situ calorimetric absorptivity measurements on bare polished 316L discs and ~100 µm powder-coated layers at 30–540 W and 100–1500 mm/s, using a 60 ± 5 µm Gaussian spot at 1070 nm (pqac-00000029). Key findings: bare-plate absorptivity in conduction mode was approximately 0.29–0.31; at the keyhole threshold (~70 W at 500 mm/s, or ~48 ± 10 W at 100 mm/s and ~108 ± 20 W at 1500 mm/s), absorptivity rose sharply and saturated at approximately 0.78 (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000027). Powder layers initially exhibited about 2× the bare-plate absorptivity, but this dropped sharply once the powder was fully melted; above the keyhole transition, powder and bare surfaces showed broadly similar absorptivity behavior, with saturation around 0.7–0.8 for steel (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026). This is a strongly supported, highly cited (662 citations) primary source.

**Spot size / defocus experiments.** Metelkova et al. (2018; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2018.08.006; 366 citations) systematically varied defocus on 316L at ±8 mm beyond the Rayleigh length, producing beam diameters of ~205 and ~262 µm, combined with P = 400–800 W and v = 50–250 mm/s (pqac-00000019). At constant P and v, changing defocus from +8 to −8 mm increased melt-pool depth by 204% while width changed only 22%; at lower power, the depth difference was smaller (+81%) (pqac-00000022). They reported a potential productivity increase of 840% (reaching 18.8 mm³/s) using a defocused hull-core strategy (pqac-00000017). Tenbrock et al. (2020; DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2019.116514; 179 citations) used top-hat beam profiles at 100, 150, and 200 µm spot diameters with 140–300 W in 316L LPBF, explicitly noting that larger raw beam diameters shorten the Rayleigh length, requiring careful beam characterization (pqac-00000016). Sow et al. (2020; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2020.101532; 254 citations) compared 80 µm Gaussian and 500 µm top-hat spots: the large spot produced shallow conduction-mode pools, suppressed vaporization and spatter, achieved near-zero porosity, and provided a 20–50% build-rate increase, while the 80 µm spot showed 0.3–0.5% porosity from keyhole instabilities (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

**Practical strategy for separating effects.** To deconfound absorptivity from beam size and from heat accumulation, the literature supports:  
(i) Varying defocus at fixed P and v to isolate beam-diameter effects (Metelkova 2018);  
(ii) Constant P/v lines at different speeds to separate linear energy density from interaction time and intensity;  
(iii) Bare-plate single tracks versus powder-on-plate single tracks to isolate powder effects (Trapp 2017);  
(iv) Single tracks versus multi-track walls versus cubes to isolate heat accumulation from neighboring tracks and layers (Zhang et al. 2021 used single tracks for calibration, then density coupons for validation).

---

### 4. Should a Second Spot Size Be Added to the First Build?

The literature strongly supports that spot size is a physically independent variable—not merely a secondary effect of VED—because it determines local intensity, Rayleigh length, keyhole onset threshold, and melt-pool aspect ratio independently of P and v (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). Metelkova et al. showed that in 316L LPBF, defocus alone can change melt-pool depth by over 200% at constant P and v (pqac-00000022). Normalized enthalpy ΔH/hs, which explicitly includes beam diameter, provides a more physically continuous relationship with melt-pool depth than VED across different speeds (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000022).

**Recommendation (moderately supported by synthesis of multiple studies):** The first build of 84 walls at a fixed 130 µm spot, with 60 P–v combinations spanning the full conduction-to-keyhole range, provides strong constraints on the E-T or Thermo-Calc AM model at that one spot size. However, without a second spot size, absorptivity and effective beam radius are confounded in any calibration: the same melt-pool geometry can be reproduced by trading one for the other (pqac-00000062). Given the practical constraint that the Concept Laser M2 has limited defocus control (beam quality, Rayleigh length, and actual delivered profile must be carefully characterized—pqac-00000016), **the safest strategy is to save a dedicated defocus build for the second build**, where it can be properly characterized with beam-caustic measurements and the initial E-T calibration can be used as a prior. If a small defocus experiment (e.g., 5–10 walls at a 50–80 µm or ~200 µm defocused spot) can be added to the first build without compromising the core design, this would provide early data on spot-size sensitivity. However, this requires verifying that the defocused spot profile is known and stable (pqac-00000016).

---

### 5. Batch Bayesian Optimization and Active Learning for LPBF

**McCarthy (2025 thesis, Ti-6Al-4V m-LPBF).** The initial design used a central composite design (CCD) with factorial, axial, and center points. Each subsequent active-learning iteration selected 24 unique feature vectors plus 8 center replicates from the CCD (pqac-00000038). The acquisition function was a greedy predictive-variance criterion (Zhao et al.'s weight information gain/expected model change maximization), applied to 1,000 randomly subsampled candidates per iteration (pqac-00000038). The study was constrained to three total prints/builds (one initial + two active-learning iterations) due to cost and timeline (pqac-00000038). Center replicates were analyzed with a fixed-effect one-way ANOVA to test whether batch significantly affected relative density (pqac-00000039). Non-dominated solutions from NSGA-II optimization were not experimentally validated (pqac-00000042).

**Pawlak (2025, AZ31 PBF-LB/M; DOI: 10.3390/app152412968).** A total of 180 samples were produced and evaluated for relative density and build rate (pqac-00000086). Three initialization strategies were compared: Latin Hypercube Sampling (V1), balanced-marginal selection (V2), and prior fractional-factorial sampling (V3), each with 20 initial samples (pqac-00000084). DGEMO and TSEMO algorithms then proposed batches of 10 parameter sets per MOBO iteration for three additional iterations (pqac-00000084). V3 (fractional-factorial initialization) achieved the highest hypervolume; TSEMO converged faster early while DGEMO explored more broadly (pqac-00000086, pqac-00000087). Critically, **60–80% of proposed candidates in some batches were duplicates** due to design-space discretization, limiting effective search diversity and causing early saturation of hypervolume improvement (pqac-00000090). The author noted that conventional PBF-LB/M campaigns typically investigate 10–20 parameter sets to identify a viable process window (pqac-00000086, pqac-00000058).

**Zhang, Parnell, Brabazon, and Benavoli (2021; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2107.12809).** In a binder-jetting 316L example, the initial design used a Taguchi L27 orthogonal array (27 settings, 4 replicates each), and BO selected batches of 2 new settings at a time (pqac-00000053). They reviewed acquisition functions including EI, qEI, UCB, KG, entropy search, Thompson sampling, and their batch extensions (qKG, dKG, bUCB) (pqac-00000055). One cited AM study initialized with a Latin-hypercube batch of 200 samples in 5D, followed by 35 MCMC-generated samples (pqac-00000055).

**Multi-fidelity BO (Dou 2025).** A multi-fidelity framework combining inexpensive and expensive thermal simulations used UCB acquisition for high-fidelity sampling and maximum posterior standard deviation for low-fidelity sampling, with a fixed high-to-low fidelity ratio r = m/n (typically n = 1 high-fidelity evaluation per iteration) (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000057).

---

### 6. Thermo-Calc AM Module and CALPHAD-Coupled Models

The Thermo-Calc AM Module provides CALPHAD-based thermophysical properties (liquidus, solidus, latent heat, density, thermal conductivity, heat capacity, surface tension, viscosity) and reportedly includes both steady-state and transient melt-pool calculations. The TAMU automated framework (Sheikh et al. 2023/2024) uses Thermo-Calc databases including TCHEA5, TCAL7, and TCNI11 to supply these properties, which are then fed to the E-T analytical model for melt-pool prediction and printability-map generation (pqac-00000033). Sjöström, Durga, and Lindwall (2022; DOI: 10.3389/fmats.2022.797226) linked Simufact Additive thermal simulations with Thermo-Calc microscale models (DICTRA) for 18Ni300 maraging steel, predicting micro-segregation and martensite-start temperature as functions of process parameters (pqac-00000037). Sargent et al. (2021; DOI: 10.3390/met11040570) used Thermo-Calc 2020b for CALPHAD-based non-equilibrium solidification modeling of SS316L, with material properties interpolated at 700 K: density 7.9 g/cm³, thermal conductivity 20.2 W/(m·K), and specific heat 470 J/(kg·K) (pqac-00000035).

**Important caveat:** No peer-reviewed independent validation of the Thermo-Calc AM Module's built-in printability-map predictions against experimental defect data was identified in the accessible literature. The available studies use Thermo-Calc primarily as a property provider rather than as an end-to-end validated printability tool. This is a **weakly supported gap**: the module may have been validated internally or in unpublished industrial work, but independent experimental benchmarks are lacking.

---

### 7. Recommendations for the Planned 84-Wall Build and Subsequent Bayesian-Optimization Builds

Based on the synthesized literature, the following design recommendations emerge:

**(a) First build (84 walls, 130 µm spot).** The 60 Sobol-sequence P–v combinations spanning P = 150–370 W and P/v = 0.09–0.55 J/mm (VED ~33–204 J/mm³) provide excellent coverage of the conduction-to-keyhole transition for a single spot size, consistent with the TAMU approach of 40–60 single-track experiments per alloy (pqac-00000082). The scrambled Sobol sequence is a space-filling quasi-random design well-suited for GP surrogate training. The 21 replicated pairs (walls printed in both orientations on the rotated fourth panel) serve dual purposes: quantifying recoater-direction effects and providing variance estimates essential for the likelihood in Bayesian calibration (cf. Trapp et al.'s repeated-track measurements, pqac-00000024). The control walls at the production parameter set provide anchor points for model validation.

**(b) Melt-pool observables.** Measuring both melt-pool width and depth from the etched last-layer cross-sections is critical for identifiability, as demonstrated by Fody et al.'s finding that absorptivity, depth, and radius are non-identifiable from width–depth data alone without additional constraints (pqac-00000062). Measuring porosity fraction in each wall core (the planned >0.2 mm from faces, >1 mm from base/top exclusion) provides the defect classification needed for printability-map validation.

**(c) Calibration approach.** Use the wall porosity and melt-pool boundary data to: (i) fit apparent absorptivity and powder-bed porosity in the E-T model following Whalen et al.'s MCMC approach, with weakly informative priors centered at A ≈ 0.35–0.68 for 316L (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000074); (ii) add a GP discrepancy function following Zhang et al.'s Kennedy–O'Hagan framework to capture systematic model–experiment differences (pqac-00000001); (iii) classify each wall as defect-free, LOF, keyhole, or balling to benchmark the Thermo-Calc AM Module's printability predictions and the Gan et al. Ke criterion (Ke > 6 for keyhole onset, pqac-00000047).

**(d) Second and later builds (Bayesian optimization).** The McCarthy (2025) precedent of 24 unique conditions + 8 center replicates per batch across 3 builds is a practical template (pqac-00000038). With 84 wall positions available per build, the budget is generous: consider allocating ~60 BO-selected conditions, ~15 replicates at a few key settings (for variance estimation and batch-effect testing), and ~5–9 hold-out points from the first build's well-characterized settings (for validating the BO surrogate's predictive accuracy). The Pawlak (2025) finding that duplicate proposals can reach 60–80% in discrete spaces argues for including a distance-based penalization in the acquisition function or using a continuous-relaxation strategy (pqac-00000090). The first build's 60 calibrated settings serve as an informative initialization for the GP surrogate—superior to cold-start approaches (pqac-00000087).

**(e) Second spot size.** Defer the second spot size to Build 2 or 3, once the 130 µm model is calibrated and the actual defocused beam profile can be measured with a beam-caustic diagnostic. Even 10–15 walls at a well-characterized ~200 µm defocused spot would break the absorptivity–spot-size degeneracy (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019). The normalized enthalpy ΔH/hs, which explicitly includes beam diameter, should be used rather than VED for cross-spot-size comparisons (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000022).

---

### Summary of Evidence Strength

| Statement | Support level |
|---|---|
| E-T absorptivity and porosity are Bayesian-calibratable from ~30 316L melt-pool depths | Strong (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002) |
| Kennedy–O'Hagan GP discrepancy improves E-T calibration | Moderate (pqac-00000001; demonstrated for Ni alloys, not yet specifically 316L with discrepancy GP) |
| Ke > 6 for keyhole onset, R² = 0.92 for porosity | Strong (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047; synchrotron-validated, 332 citations) |
| 316L printability map ~84% overall accuracy | Moderate (pqac-00000008; based on literature data, not single-machine validation) |
| VED is insufficient as a sole defect predictor for 316L | Strong (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000070; directly demonstrated) |
| 316L absorptivity: bare ~0.3, keyhole saturation ~0.78 | Strong (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000027; calorimetric measurements) |
| Defocus changes 316L melt-pool depth >200% at constant P,v | Strong (pqac-00000022; 366 citations) |
| Thermo-Calc AM Module independently validated for printability | Weak (no accessible peer-reviewed independent validation found) |
| Batch BO with ~20 init + 10/batch for 3–4 builds is practical | Moderate (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000084; different alloys and machines) |

### Key Open Datasets and Tables for Comparison

- **Kamath et al. (2014; DOI: 10.1007/s00170-014-5954-9):** 316L density data on a Concept Laser M2 with 54 µm spot, powers to 400 W—directly comparable to the user's machine (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000023).
- **Sheikh et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1038/s41524-024-01436-x):** Table 3 reports LOF accuracy for each criterion combination for 316 SS; Figure 5 shows predicted vs. experimental defect classifications (pqac-00000009).
- **Gan et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-021-22704-0):** Supplementary data include multi-material keyhole and porosity datasets; the keyhole scaling and porosity model could be directly evaluated against the planned 84-wall porosity measurements (pqac-00000046).
- **Trapp et al. (2017; DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2017.08.006):** Figures contain 316L absorptivity vs. power curves at 100, 500, and 1500 mm/s for both bare and powder-coated substrates (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025).
- **Pawlak (2025; DOI: 10.3390/app152412968):** Supplementary Table S1 contains all 180 AZ31 samples' process parameters and responses, useful as a MOBO benchmark (pqac-00000056)."}

state.question:
How have melt-pool and printability models for LPBF (analytical Eagar-Tsai, CALPHAD-coupled models such as the Thermo-Calc AM Module, finite-element and CFD) been calibrated and validated against experiments, and how should a build of 84 walls and later batch Bayesian-optimization builds be designed so the data best constrain such a model? Context: laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M, L-PBF) of commercial gas-atomized 316L stainless steel powder (about 15-45 um) on a Concept Laser M2 cusing (CL WRX Control 2.4; two 400 W class continuous-wave Yb fibre lasers at about 1070 nm, only one used; galvanometer scanner; nitrogen or argon; no plate heating; layer thickness 30 or 50 um, not yet confirmed). The machine's production 316L parameter set uses, for the core hatch, 370 W, 1350 mm/s, 0.09 mm hatch spacing and a 130 um spot (P/v = 0.274 J/mm), contours at 100-120 W and 130-220 mm/s with a 50-70 um spot, and an upskin at 200 W, 980 mm/s, 0.075 mm hatch. The build: 12 'comb' parts, each a 44.5 x 12.7 mm base (printed with the production set) carrying 7 thin walls (fins) 1.27 mm thick, 12.7 mm long and 7.6 mm tall on a 7.2 mm pitch. Every wall has its own core and upskin laser power P and scan speed v (contours unchanged): 60 settings from a scrambled Sobol sequence over P = 150-370 W and P/v = 0.09-0.55 J/mm (v about 335-2930 mm/s; about 33-204 J/mm^3 at 30 um layers), plus the production hatch as a control. ## Calibration, Validation, and Experimental Design for LPBF Melt-Pool and Printability Models: A Literature Synthesis

### 1. Bayesian Calibration of Melt-Pool Models

The following table summarizes key Bayesian calibration campaigns for LPBF melt-pool models:

| Reference | Model type | Material | Calibrated parameters | Observables | Experiments / data points | Calibration method | Key remaining discrepancy |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Whalen, Ma & Balachandran (2021), DOI: [10.1007/s40192-021-00238-z](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40192-021-00238-z) | Modified analytical Eagar–Tsai conduction model | Primarily LPBF 316L; associated analysis also considered Ti-6Al-4V and IN718 | Apparent absorptivity and powder-bed porosity/packing density; beam radius was specified rather than inferred, and effective conductivity followed from the porosity model | Predominantly single-track melt-pool depth; width and length used subsequently for geometry and printability assessment | Approximately 30 independent 316L melt-pool measurements combined from published 30 and 50 µm-layer datasets; data were partitioned by similar power and speed | Bayesian inference with constrained priors and MCMC; likelihood used a 15 µm depth standard deviation; inferred parameters were fitted as power-dependent functions | Parameter compensation and non-identifiability remain; conduction physics underpredicts depth as keyholing becomes important, and isolated experimentally conduction-classified tracks were predicted as keyhole. No explicit Kennedy–O’Hagan discrepancy GP was used. (whalen2021abayesianapproach pages 9-12, whalen2021abayesianapproach pages 16-19, whalenUnknownyearusingbayesianinference pages 3-4, whalenUnknownyearusingbayesianinferencea pages 3-4) |
| Zhang et al. (2021), DOI: [10.1016/j.addma.2021.102018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2021.102018) | Eagar–Tsai model with a GP surrogate and Bayesian model calibration/discrepancy treatment | Ni–5Nb, NiTi and AF9628 case studies; 316L data informed some property estimates | Three sensitivity-selected effective thermal inputs, including thermal conductivity and heat capacity, with absorptivity/property estimates updated against tracks; published nominal absorptivities included 0.51 for Ni–5Nb and 0.56 for NiTi | Single-track melt-pool width and depth; width averaged over nine top-view locations and depth over three etched cross-sections | Ni–5Nb: 40 tracks; NiTi: 60 tracks; three depth sections per track. A 1,000-run Eagar–Tsai ensemble trained the surrogate | Kennedy–O’Hagan-style Bayesian calibration: GP emulator plus GP model-discrepancy term and measurement error | Reported calibrated errors in one case were 3.6% MAPE for width and 4.05% for depth, but errors increased below 300 J m⁻¹ linear energy; empirical SVM/geometry boundaries were still needed for defects, limiting extrapolation. (zhang2021anefficientframework pages 4-5, zhang2021anefficientframework pages 14-16, zhang2021anefficientframework pages 12-14, zhang2021anefficientframework pages 10-12, zhang2021anefficientframework pages 9-10) |
| Fody, Leser & Narra (2025 preprint), DOI: [10.2139/ssrn.5185945](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5185945) | Three-dimensional FE thermal model with a modified symmetric Goldak volumetric Gaussian heat source | Ti-6Al-4V, bare-plate tracks on an EOS M 290 | Effective absorptivity, normalized heat-source depth and normalized heat-source radius | Cross-sectional melt-pool width and depth extracted from optical micrographs | Three P–v conditions repeated at three plate locations: 9 tracks; usable width–depth pairs were 29, 25 and 29 for the three conditions | Heteroscedastic GP emulator; six Latin-hypercube seeds plus 32 posterior-focused active-learning evaluations; SMC generated 40,000 posterior samples for one calibration | Strong posterior correlation made absorptivity, radius and depth non-identifiable without a maximum-temperature constraint. All 29 observations fell inside the 95.4% posterior-predictive contour; surrogate-to-FE validation MAPE was 0.53%, but this measures emulator fidelity rather than physical-model error. (fody2025probabilisticcalibrationof pages 5-8, fody2025probabilisticcalibrationof pages 15-20, fody2025probabilisticcalibrationof pages 23-27, fody2025probabilisticcalibrationof pages 8-12, fody2025probabilisticcalibrationof pages 34-38) |
| Saunders et al. (2022), DOI: [10.1007/s40192-022-00276-1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40192-022-00276-1) | Kennedy–O’Hagan autoregressive multifidelity GP combining lower- and higher-fidelity melt-pool models | Metal-AM melt-pool case study; the available evidence does not establish a 316L physical-calibration campaign | Cross-fidelity scaling/correlation and GP hyperparameters rather than a clearly documented physical calibration of absorptivity, beam radius, conductivity or Marangoni coefficient | Melt-pool geometry predictions and melt-regime classification | Physical experiment count and hold-out design were not established in the available evidence | Multifidelity GP surrogate in the Kennedy–O’Hagan tradition | Useful for propagating disagreement between simulation fidelities, but it should not be cited as evidence that physical heat-source parameters were uniquely calibrated against experiments unless the underlying experimental dataset is separately documented. |


*Table: Comparison of representative Bayesian and multifidelity melt-pool studies, emphasizing what was actually inferred, the experimental information used, and unresolved model discrepancy or identifiability.*

**Eagar–Tsai calibration for 316L.** Whalen, Ma, and Balachandran (2021; DOI: 10.1007/s40192-021-00238-z) performed Bayesian inference on a modified Eagar–Tsai (E-T) conduction model using approximately 30 316L single-track melt-pool depth measurements combined from the Bertoli et al. and Kamath et al. datasets (layer thicknesses 30 and 50 µm). The calibrated parameters were apparent absorptivity and powder-bed porosity; beam radius was specified (average of 55 and 52 µm from the source studies) rather than inferred (whalen2021abayesianapproach pages 9-12, whalen2021abayesianapproach pages 4-7). The likelihood assumed 15 µm depth standard deviation for measurement variability, with weakly informative normal priors: mean absorptivity of 0.68 for SS316L, mean porosity of 0.40, both constrained to [0, 1] (whalenUnknownyearusingbayesianinferencea pages 3-4). MCMC was used to generate posteriors. The fitted power-dependent absorptivity was A = 0.148 ln(P) − 0.0879 (R² = 0.77) and porosity φ = 0.0015P + 0.1626 (R² = 0.96) (whalen2021abayesianapproach pages 16-19). The principal remaining discrepancy is that conduction physics underpredicts melt-pool depth once keyholing sets in, and isolated experimental conduction-mode tracks were misclassified as keyhole (whalen2021abayesianapproach pages 16-19). No separate Kennedy–O'Hagan model-discrepancy Gaussian process was used in that work. The calibration was also performed for Ti-6Al-4V and IN718, with analogous prior absorptivities of 0.74 and 0.67, respectively (whalenUnknownyearusingbayesianinferencea pages 3-4). **This is strongly supported as the primary Bayesian E-T calibration for 316L.**

**Texas A&M (TAMU) framework.** Zhang et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2021.102018) calibrated the E-T model against single-track experiments using a Kennedy–O'Hagan-style framework: a GP surrogate trained from 1,000 E-T simulations captured forward-model behavior, and a GP discrepancy function δ(x) absorbed systematic model–experiment differences (zhang2021anefficientframework pages 4-5). Materials included Ni-5Nb (40 single tracks; absorptivity 0.51, thermal conductivity 70.4 W/(m·K), specific heat 636.19 J/(kg·K)), NiTi (60 tracks; absorptivity 0.56), and AF9628 (absorptivity approximated from published 316L measurements) (zhang2021anefficientframework pages 12-14, zhang2021anefficientframework pages 9-10). Calibrated width and depth errors for one case were 3.6% and 4.05% MAPE, respectively (zhang2021anefficientframework pages 10-12). Errors increased for linear energy density below 300 J/m, requiring additional experiments in that regime (zhang2021anefficientframework pages 10-12, zhang2021anefficientframework pages 9-10). Keyholing was classified by width-to-depth thresholds: W/D ≤ 1.2 for Ni-5Nb and W/D ≤ 2 for NiTi (zhang2021anefficientframework pages 14-16, zhang2021anefficientframework pages 10-12). Experiments were on a 3D Systems ProX 200 DMP (1070 nm fiber laser, max 260 W) under argon (zhang2021anefficientframework pages 7-9).

**FE model calibration with GP emulator.** Fody, Leser, and Narra (2025 preprint; DOI: 10.2139/ssrn.5185945) calibrated a Goldak-inspired 3D FE thermal model for Ti-6Al-4V on an EOS M 290. Three parameters were inferred: effective absorptivity (aeff), normalized heat-source depth (Ds), and normalized heat-source radius (Rs), with uniform priors on [0.01, 100], [0.8, 100], and [0.4, 10], respectively (fody2025probabilisticcalibrationof pages 8-12). Data comprised 29/25/29 melt-pool cross-section images per condition at three P–v pairs. A heteroscedastic GP emulator was trained with 6 Latin-hypercube seeds plus 32 active-learning evaluations per calibration (38 total training points), and sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) generated 40,000 posterior samples (fody2025probabilisticcalibrationof pages 15-20, fody2025probabilisticcalibrationof pages 8-12). A strong identifiability challenge required imposing a maximum-temperature constraint: without it, absorptivity, radius, and depth were highly correlated, admitting a continuous range of similarly likely posteriors (fody2025probabilisticcalibrationof pages 15-20). With the constraint, all 29 observations fell within the 95.4% posterior-predictive contour; surrogate-to-FE validation MAPE was 0.53% (fody2025probabilisticcalibrationof pages 15-20, fody2025probabilisticcalibrationof pages 23-27). Withholding ~25% of melt-pool sections produced qualitatively similar calibrations, suggesting the data budget could potentially be reduced (fody2025probabilisticcalibrationof pages 23-27).

**Practical implication for the planned build.** These studies consistently show that ~25–60 single-track or cross-section melt-pool measurements per alloy or condition are sufficient for Bayesian calibration, but the remaining discrepancy is dominated by the physics absent from conduction models (Marangoni convection, vapor depression, absorptivity transitions). Measuring both melt-pool width and depth (not just one) substantially improves parameter identifiability.
