**Texas A&M automated framework.** Sheikh et al. (2023 preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2304.04113; 2024 peer-reviewed, DOI: 10.1038/s41524-024-01436-x) constructed printability maps using CALPHAD-derived properties (Thermo-Calc databases including TCHEA5 and TCNI11) fed to the E-T model, with Gladush–Smurov correction for keyhole depth (sheikh2023anautomatedfullycomputational pages 3-5, sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 14-15). They evaluated 12 combinations of two LOF criteria, two balling criteria, and three keyhole criteria (sheikh2023anautomatedfullycomputational pages 8-10). For 316 stainless steel, evaluated against 83 literature single-track data points on a 20×15 P–v grid (beam diameter 80 µm, layer thickness 30 µm, hatch spacing 70 µm), the best combination achieved 83.96% overall accuracy (sheikh2023anautomatedfullycomputational pages 10-14). The highest LOF-specific accuracy was 87.95% (LOF1–KH3–Ball2) (sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 8-10). For NiTi, the best criterion set (Eq. 4 for LOF, Eq. 6 for balling, Eq. 10 for keyhole) achieved 84–91% accuracy across three compositions (sheikh2023anautomatedfullycomputational pages 20-25). **Balling was consistently the weakest classification**, largely because experimental balling points tended to fall near boundaries with other defect regimes (sheikh2023anautomatedfullycomputational pages 20-25). The ensemble probabilistic map weights each of the 12 combinations by its accuracy using a softmax function, so that more accurate criteria contribute more strongly (sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 5-6).

**Gan et al. Keyhole number.** Gan et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-021-22704-0) defined the dimensionless Keyhole number Ke as a function of absorbed power ηP, density ρ, heat capacity Cp, thermal diffusivity α, scan speed Vs, spot radius r0, and the liquidus-to-substrate temperature difference (Tl − T0) (gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 1-2). The regime boundaries are: conduction mode for Ke < 1.4, transition mode for 1.4 ≤ Ke ≤ 6.0, and keyhole mode for Ke > 6.0 (gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 1-2, gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 2-3). The normalized keyhole aspect ratio follows e* = 0.4(Ke − 1.4) (gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 1-2). For stability: keyhole fluctuations are small and porosity is nearly absent for Ke < 16; the keyhole becomes chaotic with significant porosity and spatter risk for Ke > 30 (gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 3-5, gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 2-3). A porosity-volume-fraction scaling law using Ke together with normalized energy density achieved R² = 0.92 across six independent literature datasets and ten process-parameter sets (gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 3-5). **This criterion applies to quasi-steady-state track interiors only**—not to scan starts, stops, or turning points (gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 6-7). This is strongly supported by synchrotron X-ray imaging and high-fidelity multiphysics simulations.

**316L-specific defect criteria.** Smith et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1007/s11837-024-06946-z) demonstrated that nine parameter sets at constant VED = 85 J/mm³ on a 3D Systems DMP Flex 350 with 316L produced systematically different defect populations, definitively showing that VED alone is not a sufficient predictor (smith2025assessingvolumetricenergy pages 1-2, smith2025assessingvolumetricenergy pages 10-11). They proposed two modifications: (i) a semi-elliptical interpass LOF criterion using measured melt-pool width and depth (replacing semicircular assumptions), and (ii) a laser-shock-pressure criterion for spatter-induced intrapass LOF at high P and high v (smith2025assessingvolumetricenergy pages 1-2, smith2025assessingvolumetricenergy pages 3-5). The modified criteria better captured defects at the low-P/low-v and high-P/high-v extremes, respectively (smith2025assessingvolumetricenergy pages 10-11). **Weakly supported: no overall classification accuracy metric was reported in the accessible portions of that paper.**

Wang, Ning, and Liang (2021; DOI: 10.3390/app112412053) provided analytical threshold predictions for Ti-6Al-4V (LOF ~110 J/mm³), IN718 (LOF ~160 J/mm³), and 316L (properties: density 7633 kg/m³, thermal conductivity 25 W/(m·°C), specific heat 594 J/(kg·°C), absorptivity 0.35), using geometric LOF (H²/W² + L²/D² ≤ 1), capillary balling (πw/l > 1), and normalized-enthalpy keyholing criteria (wang2021analyticalpredictionof pages 6-7, wang2021analyticalpredictionof pages 4-6).

---

### 3. Experiment Design for Separating Absorptivity from Spot Size and Heat Accumulation

**Absorptivity measurements for 316L.** Trapp et al. (2017; DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2017.08.006) performed in situ calorimetric absorptivity measurements on bare polished 316L discs and ~100 µm powder-coated layers at 30–540 W and 100–1500 mm/s, using a 60 ± 5 µm Gaussian spot at 1070 nm (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 2-3). Key findings: bare-plate absorptivity in conduction mode was approximately 0.29–0.31; at the keyhole threshold (~70 W at 500 mm/s, or ~48 ± 10 W at 100 mm/s and ~108 ± 20 W at 1500 mm/s), absorptivity rose sharply and saturated at approximately 0.78 (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 3-4, trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 6-7). Powder layers initially exhibited about 2× the bare-plate absorptivity, but this dropped sharply once the powder was fully melted; above the keyhole transition, powder and bare surfaces showed broadly similar absorptivity behavior, with saturation around 0.7–0.8 for steel (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 7-8, trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 1-2). This is a strongly supported, highly cited (662 citations) primary source.

**Spot size / defocus experiments.** Metelkova et al. (2018; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2018.08.006; 366 citations) systematically varied defocus on 316L at ±8 mm beyond the Rayleigh length, producing beam diameters of ~205 and ~262 µm, combined with P = 400–800 W and v = 50–250 mm/s (metelkova2018ontheinfluence pages 3-4). At constant P and v, changing defocus from +8 to −8 mm increased melt-pool depth by 204% while width changed only 22%; at lower power, the depth difference was smaller (+81%) (metelkova2018ontheinfluence pages 6-8). They reported a potential productivity increase of 840% (reaching 18.8 mm³/s) using a defocused hull-core strategy (metelkova2018ontheinfluence pages 1-3). Tenbrock et al. (2020; DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2019.116514; 179 citations) used top-hat beam profiles at 100, 150, and 200 µm spot diameters with 140–300 W in 316L LPBF, explicitly noting that larger raw beam diameters shorten the Rayleigh length, requiring careful beam characterization (tenbrock2020influenceofkeyhole pages 2-3). Sow et al. (2020; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2020.101532; 254 citations) compared 80 µm Gaussian and 500 µm top-hat spots: the large spot produced shallow conduction-mode pools, suppressed vaporization and spatter, achieved near-zero porosity, and provided a 20–50% build-rate increase, while the 80 µm spot showed 0.3–0.5% porosity from keyhole instabilities (sow2020influenceofbeam pages 7-8, sow2020influenceofbeam pages 1-3).

**Practical strategy for separating effects.** To deconfound absorptivity from beam size and from heat accumulation, the literature supports:  
(i) Varying defocus at fixed P and v to isolate beam-diameter effects (Metelkova 2018);  
(ii) Constant P/v lines at different speeds to separate linear energy density from interaction time and intensity;  
(iii) Bare-plate single tracks versus powder-on-plate single tracks to isolate powder effects (Trapp 2017);  
(iv) Single tracks versus multi-track walls versus cubes to isolate heat accumulation from neighboring tracks and layers (Zhang et al. 2021 used single tracks for calibration, then density coupons for validation).

---

### 4. Should a Second Spot Size Be Added to the First Build?

The literature strongly supports that spot size is a physically independent variable—not merely a secondary effect of VED—because it determines local intensity, Rayleigh length, keyhole onset threshold, and melt-pool aspect ratio independently of P and v (tenbrock2020influenceofkeyhole pages 2-3, metelkova2018ontheinfluence pages 3-4, sow2020influenceofbeam pages 7-8). Metelkova et al. showed that in 316L LPBF, defocus alone can change melt-pool depth by over 200% at constant P and v (metelkova2018ontheinfluence pages 6-8). Normalized enthalpy ΔH/hs, which explicitly includes beam diameter, provides a more physically continuous relationship with melt-pool depth than VED across different speeds (metelkova2018ontheinfluence pages 3-4, metelkova2018ontheinfluence pages 6-8).

**Recommendation (moderately supported by synthesis of multiple studies):** The first build of 84 walls at a fixed 130 µm spot, with 60 P–v combinations spanning the full conduction-to-keyhole range, provides strong constraints on the E-T or Thermo-Calc AM model at that one spot size. However, without a second spot size, absorptivity and effective beam radius are confounded in any calibration: the same melt-pool geometry can be reproduced by trading one for the other (fody2025probabilisticcalibrationof pages 15-20). Given the practical constraint that the Concept Laser M2 has limited defocus control (tenbrock2020influenceofkeyhole pages 2-3), **the safest strategy is to save a dedicated defocus build for the second build**, where it can be properly characterized with beam-caustic measurements and the initial E-T calibration can be used as a prior. If a small defocus experiment (e.g., 5–10 walls at a 50–80 µm or ~200 µm defocused spot) can be added to the first build without compromising the core design, this would provide early data on spot-size sensitivity. However, this requires verifying that the defocused spot profile is known and stable (tenbrock2020influenceofkeyhole pages 2-3).

---

### 5. Batch Bayesian Optimization and Active Learning for LPBF

**McCarthy (2025 thesis, Ti-6Al-4V m-LPBF).** The initial design used a central composite design (CCD) with factorial, axial, and center points. Each subsequent active-learning iteration selected 24 unique feature vectors plus 8 center replicates from the CCD (mccarthy2025surrogatebasedmultiobjectiveoptimization pages 61-65). The acquisition function was a greedy predictive-variance criterion (Zhao et al.'s weight information gain/expected model change maximization), applied to 1,000 randomly subsampled candidates per iteration (mccarthy2025surrogatebasedmultiobjectiveoptimization pages 61-65). The study was constrained to three total prints/builds (one initial + two active-learning iterations) due to cost and timeline (mccarthy2025surrogatebasedmultiobjectiveoptimization pages 61-65). Center replicates were analyzed with a fixed-effect one-way ANOVA to test whether batch significantly affected relative density (mccarthy2025surrogatebasedmultiobjectiveoptimization pages 50-56). Non-dominated solutions from NSGA-II optimization were not experimentally validated (mccarthy2025surrogatebasedmultiobjectiveoptimization pages 12-16).

**Pawlak (2025, AZ31 PBF-LB/M; DOI: 10.3390/app152412968).** A total of 180 samples were produced and evaluated for relative density and build rate (pawlak2025impactofinitialization pages 1-2). Three initialization strategies were compared: Latin Hypercube Sampling (V1), balanced-marginal selection (V2), and prior fractional-factorial sampling (V3), each with 20 initial samples (pawlak2025impactofinitialization pages 6-8). DGEMO and TSEMO algorithms then proposed batches of 10 parameter sets per MOBO iteration for three additional iterations (pawlak2025impactofinitialization pages 6-8). V3 (fractional-factorial initialization) achieved the highest hypervolume; TSEMO converged faster early while DGEMO explored more broadly (pawlak2025impactofinitialization pages 1-2, pawlak2025impactofinitialization pages 8-11). Critically, **60–80% of proposed candidates in some batches were duplicates** due to design-space discretization, limiting effective search diversity and causing early saturation of hypervolume improvement (pawlak2025impactofinitialization pages 11-13). The author noted that conventional PBF-LB/M campaigns typically investigate 10–20 parameter sets to identify a viable process window (pawlak2025impactofinitialization pages 1-2).

**Zhang, Parnell, Brabazon, and Benavoli (2021; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2107.12809).** In a binder-jetting 316L example, the initial design used a Taguchi L27 orthogonal array (27 settings, 4 replicates each), and BO selected batches of 2 new settings at a time (zhang2021bayesianoptimisationfor pages 14-16). They reviewed acquisition functions including EI, qEI, UCB, KG, entropy search, Thompson sampling, and their batch extensions (qKG, dKG, bUCB) (zhang2021bayesianoptimisationfor pages 8-11). One cited AM study initialized with a Latin-hypercube batch of 200 samples in 5D, followed by 35 MCMC-generated samples (zhang2021bayesianoptimisationfor pages 8-11).

**Multi-fidelity BO (Dou 2025).** A multi-fidelity framework combining inexpensive and expensive thermal simulations used UCB acquisition for high-fidelity sampling and maximum posterior standard deviation for low-fidelity sampling, with a fixed high-to-low fidelity ratio r = m/n (typically n = 1 high-fidelity evaluation per iteration) (dou2025smartprocessdesigna pages 88-92).

---

### 6. Thermo-Calc AM Module and CALPHAD-Coupled Models

The Thermo-Calc AM Module provides CALPHAD-based thermophysical properties (liquidus, solidus, latent heat, density, thermal conductivity, heat capacity, surface tension, viscosity) and reportedly includes both steady-state and transient melt-pool calculations. The TAMU automated framework (Sheikh et al. 2023/2024) uses Thermo-Calc databases including TCHEA5, TCAL7, and TCNI11 to supply these properties, which are then fed to the E-T analytical model for melt-pool prediction and printability-map generation (sheikh2023anautomatedfullycomputational pages 3-5). Sjöström, Durga, and Lindwall (2022; DOI: 10.3389/fmats.2022.797226) linked Simufact Additive thermal simulations with Thermo-Calc microscale models (DICTRA) for 18Ni300 maraging steel, predicting micro-segregation and martensite-start temperature as functions of process parameters (sjostrom2022linkageofmacro pages 1-2). Sargent et al. (2021; DOI: 10.3390/met11040570) used Thermo-Calc 2020b for CALPHAD-based non-equilibrium solidification modeling of SS316L, with material properties interpolated at 700 K: density 7.9 g/cm³, thermal conductivity 20.2 W/(m·K), and specific heat 470 J/(kg·K) (sargent2021integrationofprocessing pages 5-7).

**Important caveat:** No peer-reviewed independent validation of the Thermo-Calc AM Module's built-in printability-map predictions against experimental defect data was identified in the accessible literature. The available studies use Thermo-Calc primarily as a property provider rather than as an end-to-end validated printability tool. This is a **weakly supported gap**: the module may have been validated internally or in unpublished industrial work, but independent experimental benchmarks are lacking.

---

### 7. Recommendations for the Planned 84-Wall Build and Subsequent Bayesian-Optimization Builds

Based on the synthesized literature, the following design recommendations emerge:

**(a) First build (84 walls, 130 µm spot).** The 60 Sobol-sequence P–v combinations spanning P = 150–370 W and P/v = 0.09–0.55 J/mm (VED ~33–204 J/mm³) provide excellent coverage of the conduction-to-keyhole transition for a single spot size, consistent with the TAMU approach of 40–60 single-track experiments per alloy (zhang2021anefficientframework pages 9-10). The scrambled Sobol sequence is a space-filling quasi-random design well-suited for GP surrogate training. The 21 replicated pairs (walls printed in both orientations on the rotated fourth panel) serve dual purposes: quantifying recoater-direction effects and providing variance estimates essential for the likelihood in Bayesian calibration (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 3-4). The control walls at the production parameter set provide anchor points for model validation.

**(b) Melt-pool observables.** Measuring both melt-pool width and depth from the etched last-layer cross-sections is critical for identifiability, as demonstrated by Fody et al.'s finding that absorptivity, depth, and radius are non-identifiable from width–depth data alone without additional constraints (fody2025probabilisticcalibrationof pages 15-20). Measuring porosity fraction in each wall core (the planned >0.2 mm from faces, >1 mm from base/top exclusion) provides the defect classification needed for printability-map validation.

**(c) Calibration approach.** Use the wall porosity and melt-pool boundary data to: (i) fit apparent absorptivity and powder-bed porosity in the E-T model following Whalen et al.'s MCMC approach, with weakly informative priors centered at A ≈ 0.35–0.68 for 316L (whalenUnknownyearusingbayesianinferencea pages 3-4, wang2021analyticalpredictionof pages 6-7); (ii) add a GP discrepancy function following Zhang et al.'s Kennedy–O'Hagan framework to capture systematic model–experiment differences (zhang2021anefficientframework pages 4-5); (iii) classify each wall as defect-free, LOF, keyhole, or balling to benchmark the Thermo-Calc AM Module's printability predictions and the Gan et al. Ke criterion (gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 1-2).

**(d) Second and later builds (Bayesian optimization).** The McCarthy (2025) precedent of 24 unique conditions + 8 center replicates per batch across 3 builds is a practical template (mccarthy2025surrogatebasedmultiobjectiveoptimization pages 61-65). With 84 wall positions available per build, the budget is generous: consider allocating ~60 BO-selected conditions, ~15 replicates at a few key settings (for variance estimation and batch-effect testing), and ~5–9 hold-out points from the first build's well-characterized settings (for validating the BO surrogate's predictive accuracy). The Pawlak (2025) finding that duplicate proposals can reach 60–80% in discrete spaces argues for including a distance-based penalization in the acquisition function or using a continuous-relaxation strategy (pawlak2025impactofinitialization pages 11-13). The first build's 60 calibrated settings serve as an informative initialization for the GP surrogate—superior to cold-start approaches (pawlak2025impactofinitialization pages 8-11).

**(e) Second spot size.** Defer the second spot size to Build 2 or 3, once the 130 µm model is calibrated and the actual defocused beam profile can be measured with a beam-caustic diagnostic. Even 10–15 walls at a well-characterized ~200 µm defocused spot would break the absorptivity–spot-size degeneracy (tenbrock2020influenceofkeyhole pages 2-3, metelkova2018ontheinfluence pages 3-4). The normalized enthalpy ΔH/hs, which explicitly includes beam diameter, should be used rather than VED for cross-spot-size comparisons (metelkova2018ontheinfluence pages 1-3, metelkova2018ontheinfluence pages 6-8).

---

### Summary of Evidence Strength

| Statement | Support level |
|---|---|
| E-T absorptivity and porosity are Bayesian-calibratable from ~30 316L melt-pool depths | Strong (whalen2021abayesianapproach pages 9-12, whalen2021abayesianapproach pages 16-19) |
| Kennedy–O'Hagan GP discrepancy improves E-T calibration | Moderate (zhang2021anefficientframework pages 4-5) |
| Ke > 6 for keyhole onset, R² = 0.92 for porosity | Strong (gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 3-5, gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 1-2) |
| 316L printability map ~84% overall accuracy | Moderate (sheikh2023anautomatedfullycomputational pages 10-14) |
| VED is insufficient as a sole defect predictor for 316L | Strong (smith2025assessingvolumetricenergy pages 1-2, smith2025assessingvolumetricenergy pages 10-11) |
| 316L absorptivity: bare ~0.3, keyhole saturation ~0.78 | Strong (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 3-4, trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 6-7) |
| Defocus changes 316L melt-pool depth >200% at constant P,v | Strong (metelkova2018ontheinfluence pages 6-8) |
| Thermo-Calc AM Module independently validated for printability | Weak (no accessible peer-reviewed independent validation found) |
| Batch BO with ~20 init + 10/batch for 3–4 builds is practical | Moderate (mccarthy2025surrogatebasedmultiobjectiveoptimization pages 61-65, pawlak2025impactofinitialization pages 6-8) |

### Key Open Datasets and Tables for Comparison

- **Kamath et al. (2014; DOI: 10.1007/s00170-014-5954-9):** 316L density data on a Concept Laser M2 with 54 µm spot, powers to 400 W—directly comparable to the user's machine (kamath2014densityofadditivelymanufactured pages 5-7, kamath2014densityofadditivelymanufactured pages 1-5).
- **Sheikh et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1038/s41524-024-01436-x):** Table 3 reports LOF accuracy for each criterion combination for 316 SS; Figure 5 shows predicted vs. experimental defect classifications (sheikh2024anautomatedcomputational pages 8-10).
- **Gan et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-021-22704-0):** Supplementary data include multi-material keyhole and porosity datasets; the keyhole scaling and porosity model could be directly evaluated against the planned 84-wall porosity measurements (gan2021universalscalinglaws pages 3-5).
- **Trapp et al. (2017; DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2017.08.006):** Figures contain 316L absorptivity vs. power curves at 100, 500, and 1500 mm/s for both bare and powder-coated substrates (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 3-4, trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 7-8).
- **Pawlak (2025; DOI: 10.3390/app152412968):** Supplementary Table S1 contains all 180 AZ31 samples' process parameters and responses, useful as a MOBO benchmark (pawlak2025impactofinitialization pages 13-14).

### 1. Bayesian Calibration of Melt-Pool Models

(2022), DOI: [10.1007/s40192-022-00276-1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40192-022-00276-1) | Kennedy–O’Hagan autoregressive multifidelity GP combining lower- and higher-fidelity melt-pool models | Metal-AM melt-pool case study; the available evidence does not establish a 316L physical-calibration campaign | Cross-fidelity scaling/correlation and GP hyperparameters rather than a clearly documented physical calibration of absorptivity, beam radius, conductivity or Marangoni coefficient | Melt-pool geometry predictions and melt-regime classification | Physical experiment count and hold-out design were not established in the available evidence | Multifidelity GP surrogate in the Kennedy–O’Hagan tradition | Useful for propagating disagreement between simulation fidelities, but it should not be cited as evidence that physical heat-source parameters were uniquely calibrated against experiments unless the underlying experimental dataset is separately documented. |


*Table: Comparison of representative Bayesian and multifidelity melt-pool studies, emphasizing what was actually inferred, the experimental information used, and unresolved model discrepancy or identifiability.*

**Eagar–Tsai calibration for 316L.** Whalen, Ma, and Balachandran (2021; DOI: 10.1007/s40192-021-00238-z) performed Bayesian inference on a modified Eagar–Tsai (E-T) conduction model using approximately 30 316L single-track melt-pool depth measurements combined from the Bertoli et al. and Kamath et al. datasets (layer thicknesses 30 and 50 µm). The calibrated parameters were apparent absorptivity and powder-bed porosity; beam radius was specified (average of 55 and 52 µm from the source studies) rather than inferred (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000004). The likelihood assumed 15 µm depth standard deviation for measurement variability, with weakly informative normal priors: mean absorptivity of 0.68 for SS316L, mean porosity of 0.40, both constrained to [0, 1] (pqac-00000066). MCMC was used to generate posteriors. The fitted power-dependent absorptivity was A = 0.148 ln(P) − 0.0879 (R² = 0.77) and porosity φ = 0.0015P + 0.1626 (R² = 0.96) (pqac-00000002). The principal remaining discrepancy is that conduction physics underpredicts melt-pool depth once keyholing sets in, and isolated experimental conduction-mode tracks were misclassified as keyhole (pqac-00000002). No separate Kennedy–O'Hagan model-discrepancy Gaussian process was used in that work. The calibration was also performed for Ti-6Al-4V and IN718, with analogous prior absorptivities of 0.74 and 0.67, respectively (pqac-00000066). **This is strongly supported as the primary Bayesian E-T calibration for 316L.**

**Texas A&M (TAMU) framework.** Zhang et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2021.102018) calibrated the E-T model against single-track experiments using a Kennedy–O'Hagan-style framework: a GP surrogate trained from 1,000 E-T simulations captured forward-model behavior, and a GP discrepancy function δ(x) absorbed systematic model–experiment differences (pqac-00000001). Materials included Ni-5Nb (40 single tracks; absorptivity 0.51, thermal conductivity 70.4 W/(m·K), specific heat 636.19 J/(kg·K)), NiTi (60 tracks; absorptivity 0.56), and AF9628 (absorptivity approximated from published 316L measurements) (pqac-00000079, pqac-00000082). Calibrated width and depth errors for one case were 3.6% and 4.05% MAPE, respectively (pqac-00000080). Errors increased for linear energy density below 300 J/m, requiring additional experiments in that regime (pqac-00000080, pqac-00000082). Keyholing was classified by width-to-depth thresholds: W/D ≤ 1.2 for Ni-5Nb and W/D ≤ 2 for NiTi (pqac-00000077, pqac-00000080). Experiments were on a 3D Systems ProX 200 DMP (1070 nm fiber laser, max 260 W) under argon (pqac-00000078).

**FE model calibration with GP emulator.** Fody, Leser, and Narra (2025 preprint; DOI: 10.2139/ssrn.5185945) calibrated a Goldak-inspired 3D FE thermal model for Ti-6Al-4V on an EOS M 290. Three parameters were inferred: effective absorptivity (aeff), normalized heat-source depth (Ds), and normalized heat-source radius (Rs), with uniform priors on [0.01, 100], [0.8, 100], and [0.4, 10], respectively (pqac-00000067). Data comprised 29/25/29 melt-pool cross-section images per condition at three P–v pairs. A heteroscedastic GP emulator was trained with 6 Latin-hypercube seeds plus 32 active-learning evaluations per calibration (38 total training points), and sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) generated 40,000 posterior samples (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000067). A strong identifiability challenge required imposing a maximum-temperature constraint: without it, absorptivity, radius, and depth were highly correlated, admitting a continuous range of similarly likely posteriors (pqac-00000062). With the constraint, all 29 observations fell within the 95.4% posterior-predictive contour; surrogate-to-FE validation MAPE was 0.53% (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000064). Withholding ~25% of melt-pool sections produced qualitatively similar calibrations, suggesting the data budget could potentially be reduced (pqac-00000064).

**Practical implication for the planned build.** These studies consistently show that ~25–60 single-track or cross-section melt-pool measurements per alloy or condition are sufficient for Bayesian calibration, but the remaining discrepancy is dominated by the physics absent from conduction models (Marangoni convection, vapor depression, absorptivity transitions). Measuring both melt-pool width and depth (not just one) substantially improves parameter identifiability.

The ensemble probabilistic map weights each of the 12 combinations by its accuracy using a softmax function, so that more accurate criteria contribute more strongly (pqac-00000013).

**Gan et al. Keyhole number.** Gan et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-021-22704-0) defined the dimensionless Keyhole number Ke as a function of absorbed power ηP, density ρ, heat capacity Cp, thermal diffusivity α, scan speed Vs, spot radius r0, and the liquidus-to-substrate temperature difference (Tl − T0) (pqac-00000047). The regime boundaries are: conduction mode for Ke < 1.4, transition mode for 1.4 ≤ Ke ≤ 6.0, and keyhole mode for Ke > 6.0 (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049). The normalized keyhole aspect ratio follows e* = 0.4(Ke − 1.4) (pqac-00000047). For stability: keyhole fluctuations are small and porosity is nearly absent for Ke < 16; the keyhole becomes chaotic with significant porosity and spatter risk for Ke > 30 (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000049). A porosity-volume-fraction scaling law using Ke together with normalized energy density achieved R² = 0.92 across six independent literature datasets and ten process-parameter sets (pqac-00000046). **This criterion applies to quasi-steady-state track interiors only**—not to scan starts, stops, or turning points (pqac-00000051). This is strongly supported by synchrotron X-ray imaging and high-fidelity multiphysics simulations.

**316L-specific defect criteria.** Smith et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1007/s11837-024-06946-z) demonstrated that nine parameter sets at constant VED = 85 J/mm³ on a 3D Systems DMP Flex 350 with 316L produced systematically different defect populations, definitively showing that VED alone is not a sufficient predictor (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000070). They proposed two modifications: (i) a semi-elliptical interpass LOF criterion using measured melt-pool width and depth (replacing semicircular assumptions), and (ii) a laser-shock-pressure criterion for spatter-induced intrapass LOF at high P and high v (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000073). The modified criteria better captured defects at the low-P/low-v and high-P/high-v extremes, respectively (pqac-00000070). **Weakly supported: no overall classification accuracy metric was reported in the accessible portions of that paper.**

Wang, Ning, and Liang (2021; DOI: 10.3390/app112412053) provided analytical threshold predictions for Ti-6Al-4V (LOF ~110 J/mm³), IN718 (LOF ~160 J/mm³), and 316L (properties: density 7633 kg/m³, thermal conductivity 25 W/(m·°C), specific heat 594 J/(kg·°C), absorptivity 0.35), using geometric LOF (H²/W² + L²/D² ≤ 1), capillary balling (πw/l > 1), and normalized-enthalpy keyholing criteria (pqac-00000074, pqac-00000076).

---

### 3. Experiment Design for Separating Absorptivity from Spot Size and Heat Accumulation

**Absorptivity measurements for 316L.** Trapp et al. (2017; DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2017.08.006) performed in situ calorimetric absorptivity measurements on bare polished 316L discs and ~100 µm powder-coated layers at 30–540 W and 100–1500 mm/s, using a 60 ± 5 µm Gaussian spot at 1070 nm (pqac-00000029). Key findings: bare-plate absorptivity in conduction mode was approximately 0.29–0.31; at the keyhole threshold (~70 W at 500 mm/s, or ~48 ± 10 W at 100 mm/s and ~108 ± 20 W at 1500 mm/s), absorptivity rose sharply and saturated at approximately 0.78 (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000027). Powder layers initially exhibited about 2× the bare-plate absorptivity, but this dropped sharply once the powder was fully melted; above the keyhole transition, powder and bare surfaces showed broadly similar absorptivity behavior, with saturation around 0.7–0.8 for steel (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026). This is a strongly supported, highly cited (662 citations) primary source.

**Spot size / defocus experiments.** Metelkova et al. (2018; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2018.08.006; 366 citations) systematically varied defocus on 316L at ±8 mm beyond the Rayleigh length, producing beam diameters of ~205 and ~262 µm, combined with P = 400–800 W and v = 50–250 mm/s (pqac-00000019). At constant P and v, changing defocus from +8 to −8 mm increased melt-pool depth by 204% while width changed only 22%; at lower power, the depth difference was smaller (+81%) (pqac-00000022). They reported a potential productivity increase of 840% (reaching 18.8 mm³/s) using a defocused hull-core strategy (pqac-00000017). Tenbrock et al. (2020; DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2019.116514; 179 citations) used top-hat beam profiles at 100, 150, and 200 µm spot diameters with 140–300 W in 316L LPBF, explicitly noting that larger raw beam diameters shorten the Rayleigh length, requiring careful beam characterization (pqac-00000016). Sow et al. (2020; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2020.101532; 254 citations) compared 80 µm Gaussian and 500 µm top-hat spots: the large spot produced shallow conduction-mode pools, suppressed vaporization and spatter, achieved near-zero porosity, and provided a 20–50% build-rate increase, while the 80 µm spot showed 0.3–0.5% porosity from keyhole instabilities (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

**Practical strategy for separating effects.** To deconfound absorptivity from beam size and from heat accumulation, the literature supports:  
(i) Varying defocus at fixed P and v to isolate beam-diameter effects (Metelkova 2018);  
(ii) Constant P/v lines at different speeds to separate linear energy density from interaction time and intensity;  
(iii) Bare-plate single tracks versus powder-on-plate single tracks to isolate powder effects (Trapp 2017);  
(iv) Single tracks versus multi-track walls versus cubes to isolate heat accumulation from neighboring tracks and layers (Zhang et al. 2021 used single tracks for calibration, then density coupons for validation).

---

### 4. Should a Second Spot Size Be Added to the First Build?

The literature strongly supports that spot size is a physically independent variable—not merely a secondary effect of VED—because it determines local intensity, Rayleigh length, keyhole onset threshold, and melt-pool aspect ratio independently of P and v (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). Metelkova et al. showed that in 316L LPBF, defocus alone can change melt-pool depth by over 200% at constant P and v (pqac-00000022). Normalized enthalpy ΔH/hs, which explicitly includes beam diameter, provides a more physically continuous relationship with melt-pool depth than VED across different speeds (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000022).

**Recommendation (moderately supported by synthesis of multiple studies):** The first build of 84 walls at a fixed 130 µm spot, with 60 P–v combinations spanning the full conduction-to-keyhole range, provides strong constraints on the E-T or Thermo-Calc AM model at that one spot size. However, without a second spot size, absorptivity and effective beam radius are confounded in any calibration: the same melt-pool geometry can be reproduced by trading one for the other (pqac-00000062). Given the practical constraint that the Concept Laser M2 has limited defocus control (beam quality, Rayleigh length, and actual delivered profile must be carefully characterized—pqac-00000016), **the safest strategy is to save a dedicated defocus build for the second build**, where it can be properly characterized with beam-caustic measurements and the initial E-T calibration can be used as a prior. If a small defocus experiment (e.g., 5–10 walls at a 50–80 µm or ~200 µm defocused spot) can be added to the first build without compromising the core design, this would provide early data on spot-size sensitivity. However, this requires verifying that the defocused spot profile is known and stable (pqac-00000016).

---

### 5. Batch Bayesian Optimization and Active Learning for LPBF

**McCarthy (2025 thesis, Ti-6Al-4V m-LPBF).** The initial design used a central composite design (CCD) with factorial, axial, and center points. Each subsequent active-learning iteration selected 24 unique feature vectors plus 8 center replicates from the CCD (pqac-00000038). The acquisition function was a greedy predictive-variance criterion (Zhao et al.'s weight information gain/expected model change maximization), applied to 1,000 randomly subsampled candidates per iteration (pqac-00000038). The study was constrained to three total prints/builds (one initial + two active-learning iterations) due to cost and timeline (pqac-00000038). Center replicates were analyzed with a fixed-effect one-way ANOVA to test whether batch significantly affected relative density (pqac-00000039). Non-dominated solutions from NSGA-II optimization were not experimentally validated (pqac-00000042).

**Pawlak (2025, AZ31 PBF-LB/M; DOI: 10.3390/app152412968).** A total of 180 samples were produced and evaluated for relative density and build rate (pqac-00000086). Three initialization strategies were compared: Latin Hypercube Sampling (V1), balanced-marginal selection (V2), and prior fractional-factorial sampling (V3), each with 20 initial samples (pqac-00000084). DGEMO and TSEMO algorithms then proposed batches of 10 parameter sets per MOBO iteration for three additional iterations (pqac-00000084). V3 (fractional-factorial initialization) achieved the highest hypervolume; TSEMO converged faster early while DGEMO explored more broadly (pqac-00000086, pqac-00000087). Critically, **60–80% of proposed candidates in some batches were duplicates** due to design-space discretization, limiting effective search diversity and causing early saturation of hypervolume improvement (pqac-00000090). The author noted that conventional PBF-LB/M campaigns typically investigate 10–20 parameter sets to identify a viable process window (pqac-00000086, pqac-00000058).

**Zhang, Parnell, Brabazon, and Benavoli (2021; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2107.12809).** In a binder-jetting 316L example, the initial design used a Taguchi L27 orthogonal array (27 settings, 4 replicates each), and BO selected batches of 2 new settings at a time (pqac-00000053). They reviewed acquisition functions including EI, qEI, UCB, KG, entropy search, Thompson sampling, and their batch extensions (qKG, dKG, bUCB) (pqac-00000055). One cited AM study initialized with a Latin-hypercube batch of 200 samples in 5D, followed by 35 MCMC-generated samples (pqac-00000055).

**Multi-fidelity BO (Dou 2025).** A multi-fidelity framework combining inexpensive and expensive thermal simulations used UCB acquisition for high-fidelity sampling and maximum posterior standard deviation for low-fidelity sampling, with a fixed high-to-low fidelity ratio r = m/n (typically n = 1 high-fidelity evaluation per iteration) (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000057).

---

### 6. Thermo-Calc AM Module and CALPHAD-Coupled Models

The Thermo-Calc AM Module provides CALPHAD-based thermophysical properties (liquidus, solidus, latent heat, density, thermal conductivity, heat capacity, surface tension, viscosity) and reportedly includes both steady-state and transient melt-pool calculations. The TAMU automated framework (Sheikh et al. 2023/2024) uses Thermo-Calc databases including TCHEA5, TCAL7, and TCNI11 to supply these properties, which are then fed to the E-T analytical model for melt-pool prediction and printability-map generation (pqac-00000033). Sjöström, Durga, and Lindwall (2022; DOI: 10.3389/fmats.2022.797226) linked Simufact Additive thermal simulations with Thermo-Calc microscale models (DICTRA) for 18Ni300 maraging steel, predicting micro-segregation and martensite-start temperature as functions of process parameters (pqac-00000037). Sargent et al. (2021; DOI: 10.3390/met11040570) used Thermo-Calc 2020b for CALPHAD-based non-equilibrium solidification modeling of SS316L, with material properties interpolated at 700 K: density 7.9 g/cm³, thermal conductivity 20.2 W/(m·K), and specific heat 470 J/(kg·K) (pqac-00000035).

**Important caveat:** No peer-reviewed independent validation of the Thermo-Calc AM Module's built-in printability-map predictions against experimental defect data was identified in the accessible literature. The available studies use Thermo-Calc primarily as a property provider rather than as an end-to-end validated printability tool. This is a **weakly supported gap**: the module may have been validated internally or in unpublished industrial work, but independent experimental benchmarks are lacking.

---

### 7. Recommendations for the Planned 84-Wall Build and Subsequent Bayesian-Optimization Builds

Based on the synthesized literature, the following design recommendations emerge:

**(a) First build (84 walls, 130 µm spot).** The 60 Sobol-sequence P–v combinations spanning P = 150–370 W and P/v = 0.09–0.55 J/mm (VED ~33–204 J/mm³) provide excellent coverage of the conduction-to-keyhole transition for a single spot size, consistent with the TAMU approach of 40–60 single-track experiments per alloy (pqac-00000082). The scrambled Sobol sequence is a space-filling quasi-random design well-suited for GP surrogate training. The 21 replicated pairs (walls printed in both orientations on the rotated fourth panel) serve dual purposes: quantifying recoater-direction effects and providing variance estimates essential for the likelihood in Bayesian calibration (cf. Trapp et al.'s repeated-track measurements, pqac-00000024). The control walls at the production parameter set provide anchor points for model validation.

**(b) Melt-pool observables.** Measuring both melt-pool width and depth from the etched last-layer cross-sections is critical for identifiability, as demonstrated by Fody et al.'s finding that absorptivity, depth, and radius are non-identifiable from width–depth data alone without additional constraints (pqac-00000062). Measuring porosity fraction in each wall core (the planned >0.2 mm from faces, >1 mm from base/top exclusion) provides the defect classification needed for printability-map validation.

**(c) Calibration approach.** Use the wall porosity and melt-pool boundary data to: (i) fit apparent absorptivity and powder-bed porosity in the E-T model following Whalen et al.'s MCMC approach, with weakly informative priors centered at A ≈ 0.35–0.68 for 316L (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000074); (ii) add a GP discrepancy function following Zhang et al.'s Kennedy–O'Hagan framework to capture systematic model–experiment differences (pqac-00000001); (iii) classify each wall as defect-free, LOF, keyhole, or balling to benchmark the Thermo-Calc AM Module's printability predictions and the Gan et al. Ke criterion (Ke > 6 for keyhole onset, pqac-00000047).

**(d) Second and later builds (Bayesian optimization).** The McCarthy (2025) precedent of 24 unique conditions + 8 center replicates per batch across 3 builds is a practical template (pqac-00000038). With 84 wall positions available per build, the budget is generous: consider allocating ~60 BO-selected conditions, ~15 replicates at a few key settings (for variance estimation and batch-effect testing), and ~5–9 hold-out points from the first build's well-characterized settings (for validating the BO surrogate's predictive accuracy). The Pawlak (2025) finding that duplicate proposals can reach 60–80% in discrete spaces argues for including a distance-based penalization in the acquisition function or using a continuous-relaxation strategy (pqac-00000090). The first build's 60 calibrated settings serve as an informative initialization for the GP surrogate—superior to cold-start approaches (pqac-00000087).

**(e) Second spot size.** Defer the second spot size to Build 2 or 3, once the 130 µm model is calibrated and the actual defocused beam profile can be measured with a beam-caustic diagnostic. Even 10–15 walls at a well-characterized ~200 µm defocused spot would break the absorptivity–spot-size degeneracy (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019). The normalized enthalpy ΔH/hs, which explicitly includes beam diameter, should be used rather than VED for cross-spot-size comparisons (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000022).

---

### Summary of Evidence Strength

| Statement | Support level |
|---|---|
| E-T absorptivity and porosity are Bayesian-calibratable from ~30 316L melt-pool depths | Strong (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002) |
| Kennedy–O'Hagan GP discrepancy improves E-T calibration | Moderate (pqac-00000001; demonstrated for Ni alloys, not yet specifically 316L with discrepancy GP) |
| Ke > 6 for keyhole onset, R² = 0.92 for porosity | Strong (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047; synchrotron-validated, 332 citations) |
| 316L printability map ~84% overall accuracy | Moderate (pqac-00000008; based on literature data, not single-machine validation) |
| VED is insufficient as a sole defect predictor for 316L | Strong (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000070; directly demonstrated) |
| 316L absorptivity: bare ~0.3, keyhole saturation ~0.78 | Strong (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000027; calorimetric measurements) |
| Defocus changes 316L melt-pool depth >200% at constant P,v | Strong (pqac-00000022; 366 citations) |
| Thermo-Calc AM Module independently validated for printability | Weak (no accessible peer-reviewed independent validation found) |
| Batch BO with ~20 init + 10/batch for 3–4 builds is practical | Moderate (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000084; different alloys and machines) |

### Key Open Datasets and Tables for Comparison

- **Kamath et al. (2014; DOI: 10.1007/s00170-014-5954-9):** 316L density data on a Concept Laser M2 with 54 µm spot, powers to 400 W—directly comparable to the user's machine (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000023).
- **Sheikh et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1038/s41524-024-01436-x):** Table 3 reports LOF accuracy for each criterion combination for 316 SS; Figure 5 shows predicted vs. experimental defect classifications (pqac-00000009).
- **Gan et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-021-22704-0):** Supplementary data include multi-material keyhole and porosity datasets; the keyhole scaling and porosity model could be directly evaluated against the planned 84-wall porosity measurements (pqac-00000046).
- **Trapp et al. (2017; DOI: 10.1016/j.apmt.2017.08.006):** Figures contain 316L absorptivity vs. power curves at 100, 500, and 1500 mm/s for both bare and powder-coated substrates (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025).
- **Pawlak (2025; DOI: 10.3390/app152412968):** Supplementary Table S1 contains all 180 AZ31 samples' process parameters and responses, useful as a MOBO benchmark (pqac-00000056).

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the Texas A&M automated, fully computational framework for constructing additive-manufacturing printability maps. It uses the E-T analytical moving Gaussian heat-source model to predict melt-pool length, width, and depth from laser power, scan speed, beam size, and thermophysical properties. Because E-T underestimates depth after the transition to keyhole mode, the framework uses the Gladush–Smurov model to correct keyhole melt-pool depth. Defect regions are generated by combining criteria for lack of fusion, balling, and keyholing, then projecting their union into a two-dimensional processing map. The framework evaluates alternative criteria as binary classifiers using precision, recall, and overall accuracy, with predictions compared against experimental data. Lack of fusion is assessed using either melt-pool depth relative to powder-layer thickness or a hatch-spacing/maximum-overlap condition. Balling is evaluated using melt-pool length-to-width ratios, including a threshold of 2.3 and a second Plateau–Rayleigh-based criterion. Keyholing is associated with high laser power and low scan speed and is evaluated using depth-to-width thresholds; the excerpt states thresholds of 2.0 for NiTi and 2.75 for general alloys. The provided pages do not identify which criterion performed best specifically for 316L stainless steel, report boundary accuracy against experiments, or define a separate keyhole-number criterion.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the Texas A&M automated, fully computational framework for constructing and evaluating additive-manufacturing printability maps. For each alloy system, the framework combines two lack-of-fusion criteria, two balling criteria, and three keyholing criteria, producing 12 possible printability-map combinations. The keyholing options include a melt-pool geometry criterion (KH1), a normalized-enthalpy criterion (KH2), and Gan et al.’s dimensionless keyhole-number criterion (KH3). The keyhole number is Ke, calculated from laser power, scan speed, beam radius, absorptivity, liquidus and substrate temperatures, density, heat capacity, and thermal diffusivity; the cited threshold for keyhole mode in L-PBF is Ke > 6. For general AM alloys, the geometry threshold is W/D ≤ 2.75, while the excerpt notes a NiTi-specific threshold of 2.0. Experimental points from in-house L-PBF data are superimposed on each map to evaluate how well model-and-criterion combinations identify defect regions. Performance is assessed as binary classification using precision, recall, and accuracy. The preferred combination is selected using the highest weighted average accuracy across four binary classification cases, while precision and recall are also reported. This excerpt establishes the evaluation method but does not provide the specific 316L results, the winning criterion combination, or numerical boundary accuracy against experiments.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the automated, fully computational printability-map framework developed by Sheikh and collaborators, associated with Texas A&M University. The framework is intended to evaluate laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) printability for arbitrary alloy chemistries and to classify macroscopic defects including lack of fusion, keyholing, and balling. Its workflow has four stages: calculating thermophysical properties, calculating melt-pool dimensions, selecting defect-onset criteria, and constructing the map. Alloy chemistry and process-window inputs, such as laser power and scan speed ranges, are required. Thermo-Calc/CALPHAD models provide properties including liquidus and solidus temperatures, latent heat, heat capacity, thermal conductivity, viscosity, density, and surface tension; rule-of-mixtures calculations provide additional representative properties. Melt-pool geometry is computed with the Eagar–Tsai analytical thermal model using material properties, laser power, scan speed, beam diameter, and absorptivity. The authors state that they benchmarked 12 different defect criteria against an extensive validation dataset. However, these pages do not identify which criterion performed best for 316L stainless steel, do not provide the specific keyhole-number formulation or its selected threshold, and do not report numerical boundary accuracy relative to experiments. They only establish the framework and its modeling components; the requested comparative results must come from later results/discussion pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a 316L LPBF study designed specifically to separate the effects of laser power and spot diameter on melting mode, melt-pool geometry, and process efficiency. It used Top-Hat-like beam profiles with spot diameters of 100, 150, and 200 μm and laser powers of 140, 200, 250, and 300 W. This provides direct precedent for adding a second spot size when studying variations in power and scanning speed, particularly if the objectives include melt-pool depth, density, keyhole onset, or productivity. Spot diameter changes the intensity distribution at a given power and therefore can alter the transition between conduction and keyhole melting; it also changes the effective energy density and interaction-zone dimensions. The study emphasizes that LPBF keyholes are only several hundred micrometers deep, so the beam profile may influence the entire melt region. It also reports that larger raw beam diameters shorten the Rayleigh length, making the process more sensitive to focal-plane position. Consequently, comparisons between spot sizes require careful control and characterization of focus, actual power in the process plane, beam quality, and thermal stabilization. The excerpt does not provide quantitative density, depth, or keyhole-onset results, so those effects would need to be measured experimentally.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that laser spot size and defocus should be treated as important experimental variables alongside laser power and scanning speed in LPBF of 316L. Increasing spot size can raise build productivity, but may reduce dimensional precision and surface quality. The authors use defocus within a hull-core strategy: a larger, defocused spot supports high-productivity core scanning, while a smaller focused spot is retained for accurate hull scanning. Melt-pool morphology and process stability depend strongly on heat input. Too little heat input or excessive scanning speed can cause discontinuous balling, whereas heat input above a setup-dependent threshold can trigger keyhole-mode melting and associated spherical voids. The study links melt-pool depth to normalized enthalpy and melt-pool width to the Rosenthal equation, suggesting that comparisons across spot sizes should account for absorptivity, thermal diffusivity, melting enthalpy, layer thickness, and beam diameter rather than relying only on power and speed. The reported defocus strategy produced a potential productivity increase of 840%, reaching 18.8 mm³/s. Thus, the excerpt provides a rationale for adding a second spot-size or defocus condition when studying the effects of P and v, while keeping other relevant geometric and thermal parameters controlled.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that laser defocus can strongly alter melt-pool depth even when laser power and scanning speed are held constant, while its effect on width is generally much smaller. The influence of defocus sign becomes stronger at higher power and lower scanning speed: under one reported condition, changing defocus from +8 mm to −8 mm increased depth by 204%, whereas width changed by only 22%. At lower power and higher speed, the depth difference was smaller (+81%) and width remained comparable. These results imply that experiments varying P and v should control or systematically vary spot size/defocus, because otherwise changes attributed to power or speed may be confounded by beam geometry and depth-dependent keyhole behavior. The excerpt also suggests that conventional VED does not always produce a continuous relationship with melt-pool depth, particularly at low scan speeds, whereas normalized enthalpy using spot size gives a more continuous trend across speeds. Thus, a second spot size could be useful if the goal is to distinguish defocus effects from P–v effects and assess robustness across beam diameters. However, this excerpt does not directly quantify powder-bed density, productivity, or the precise onset threshold of keyhole melting; those require additional measurements and experiments.

For top-hat beams with spot diameters from 100 to 200 μm, the study links spot size and beam intensity to line energy, melt-pool geometry, melting mechanism, density, and process efficiency. contexts.context: The excerpt describes an LPBF experimental design for AISI 316L powder (10–45 μm grain fraction) using spot diameters of 100, 150, and 200 μm, laser powers of 140, 200, 250, and 300 W, and scan speeds from 150 to 1500 mm/s. This design directly supports evaluating how spot size interacts with laser power and scan speed in determining melt-pool geometry and process regime. Melt-pool width and depth were measured from etched cross-sections, and the aspect ratio was calculated as depth divided by width. Keyhole melting was classified at an aspect ratio above 0.8, while conduction-mode melting was classified below 0.8; transition and unstable tracks were also identified separately. Each parameter combination used duplicate vectors and multiple cross-section measurements, with a 50 μm powder layer. The excerpt therefore provides a useful precedent for adding a second or additional spot size when studying variations in P and v, especially if the goal is to resolve melt-pool depth, keyhole onset, and stability. However, these pages describe the methodology rather than quantitative effects on density, productivity, or defocus. contexts.context: The excerpt addresses single-track absorptivity for bare metallic discs, including 316L steel, rather than directly presenting the bare-plate-versus-powder comparison. For steel, regime I shows relatively small absorptivity changes before keyholing; depending on scan speed, absorptivity can increase or decrease as power rises. Melting is observed under the investigated steel conditions, with calculated melting powers of approximately 26/24 W for 100 mm s−1 and 42/41 W for 1500 mm s−1, while experimentally observed melting occurs below 30 W. The transition to regime II is associated with the onset of deep penetration/keyhole formation. Experimentally observed boiling/keyhole thresholds are approximately 48 ± 10 W at 100 mm s−1 and 108 ± 20 W at 1500 mm s−1. The calculated boiling powers are lower, about 26/24 W and 42/41 W, respectively; the model underpredicts the measured threshold by roughly a factor of 2, partly because recoil pressure must overcome melt-pool surface tension. Once the temperature exceeds boiling, vapor recoil forms a keyhole and multiple reflections from its walls sharply increase absorption. At higher powers, absorptivity saturates below unity, reaching roughly 0.7–0.8 for steel.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes in situ optical measurements performed on AISI 316L hot-rolled plates rather than on a powder bed. The experiments generated individual melt tracks, with reflected laser radiation monitored using an integrating sphere and laser-output fluctuations tracked through a back-reflection signal. The integrating-sphere signal was processed by excluding the first and last 5% of each track because these regions corresponded to melt-pool initiation and laser shutoff. Although the study refers to changes in absorption, it explicitly treats the result as a qualitative reflection-based assessment, not a quantitative absorptivity measurement. The geometry of the integrating sphere does not capture all reflected radiation, so absorption cannot be calculated directly from the reflection signal. Consequently, this excerpt does not provide separate absorptivity values for bare 316L plate versus powder, does not report a single-track powder-bed absorptivity, does not identify a keyhole-transition absorptivity, and does not include absorptivity values attributed to Trapp et al. It is therefore useful mainly for distinguishing a bare-plate, single-melt-track qualitative reflection experiment from quantitative LPBF absorptivity studies.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative, rather than numerical, findings about in situ absorptivity during laser powder-bed fusion. Before melting, the powder layer exhibits high absorptivity. Once the powder on a scanned track is completely molten, the absorptivity of the powder-coated surface becomes qualitatively comparable to that of a flat or bare substrate. When a keyhole forms, absorptivity increases. The authors also report that scanning speed affects the process and that the powder layer attenuates the influence of scanning speed on absorptivity compared with bare discs. The transition from conduction to keyhole mode cannot be reliably estimated from peak-temperature calculations alone because local evaporation and liquid-metal surface tension must be considered. The excerpt states that complete melting of the powder track and underlying substrate is needed for full bonding, while the low density and thermal isolation of individual particles facilitate powder-layer melting; consequently, powder absorptivity has a smaller role near the keyhole regime. Although the question asks for 316L bare-plate-versus-powder absorptivity values and the keyhole-transition value, no numerical 316L measurements or transition thresholds appear in this excerpt. contexts.context: The excerpt describes Trapp et al.’s direct calorimetric measurements of effective absorptivity for 316L stainless steel during laser powder-bed-fusion-relevant conditions. Measurements used continuous-wave 1070 nm laser light over approximately 30–540 W and scanning speeds of 100, 500, and 1500 mm/s, comparing bare polished discs with approximately 100 μm powder-coated layers. The supplied pages do not provide numerical absorptivity values in absolute units, but they report the key relative result: at low laser power, the powder-layer absorptivity was about twice that of the bare polished disc. For bare plates, absorptivity changed only slightly with increasing power until recoil pressure produced a surface depression; the resulting morphology increased absorption. For powder tracks, absorptivity dropped sharply once the powder was fully melted, then increased at higher power as a keyhole formed, qualitatively resembling the bare-disc behavior. Above the keyhole transition, absorptivity approached a saturation value for both bare and powder-coated samples. Thus, the study indicates that 316L absorptivity is strongly dependent on powder versus solid surface state, laser power, melting, and keyhole formation, rather than being a constant material property. The excerpt mentions single- and multi-track experiments but does not give their specific numerical values.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to computational melt-pool calculation and printability-map construction, although it does not specifically describe the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing AM Module, transient calculations, experimental validation, or 316L results. The framework uses CALPHAD-derived and rule-of-mixtures material properties to estimate single-track melt-pool geometry with the analytical Eagar–Tsai model. Required inputs include thermal conductivity, thermal diffusivity, density, specific heat, liquidus temperature, laser power, and scan speed. Because Eagar–Tsai assumes temperature-independent properties, conductivity and density are evaluated at the liquidus temperature, while effective specific heat represents heat absorption during heating and melting. Melt-pool length, width, and depth are obtained from the region reaching the alloy melting temperature. Since Eagar–Tsai underestimates depth in keyhole mode, the Gladush–Smurov model supplies a corrected depth based on processing and thermophysical parameters. This corrected depth is used to assess lack of fusion and balling criteria and define defect regions in printability maps. The authors acknowledge that both analytical models neglect fluid flow, including Marangoni convection, and temperature-dependent properties, limiting accuracy under keyholing and high-speed laser powder bed fusion conditions.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a fully computational additive-manufacturing printability-map framework built around four stages: calculating thermophysical properties, calculating melt-pool dimensions, selecting defect criteria, and constructing the map. Thermo-Calc is used to obtain CALPHAD-based properties through Property, Equilibrium, and Scheil models, with databases including TCHEA5, TCAL7, and TCNI11. Calculated quantities include liquidus and solidus temperatures, latent heat, heat capacity, thermal conductivity, diffusivity, density, viscosity, surface tension, enthalpy, and related derived attributes. Melt-pool dimensions for laser powder-bed fusion are calculated using the Eagar–Tsai analytical model, which predicts quasi-steady-state temperature fields and melt-pool isotherms from material properties and processing conditions such as laser power, scan speed, and beam diameter. The framework proposes criteria for lack of fusion, keyholing, and balling, benchmarks 12 defect-onset criteria, and compares resulting maps with an extensive experimental validation dataset. The excerpt does not provide specific results for 316L, nor does it describe a separate transient melt-pool calculation or explicitly identify a Thermo-Calc AM Module interface; its melt-pool treatment is primarily Eagar–Tsai and quasi-steady-state.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a pool-based batch active-learning strategy for LPBF rather than sequential sampling. The acquisition method is Zhao et al.’s weight information gain/expected model change maximization, implemented approximately through a greedy algorithm. Because the full unlabeled design space was too large, 1,000 candidate feature vectors were randomly subsampled from the unlabeled pool at every iteration. The greedy procedure repeatedly selects the candidate maximizing ρ(x), removes it from the candidate set, and updates the selected set; the criterion is equivalent to predictive variance without the additional noise variance and accounts for correlations among already selected points. A maximum-a-posteriori estimate of the Gaussian-process hyperparameters was used to evaluate the acquisition function, with a constant noise term included but not affecting the ranking. Each active-learning iteration selected 24 unique feature vectors and included 8 center replicates from the central composite design (CCD). Due to LPBF cost and project timeline, the experiment comprised at most three prints/builds: one initial print followed by two active-learning iterations. The excerpt does not specify hold-out points or a separate validation set. It also does not provide the initial CCD’s total run count, although it explicitly identifies center replicates as part of the iterative design.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an active-learning experimental strategy for Ti-6Al-4V laser powder bed fusion, but it does not report specific Bayesian optimization batch sizes, acquisition functions, total numbers of builds, hold-out points, or a prescribed number of active-learning iterations. The initial experiment used a central composite design (CCD), comprising factorial points, axial points, and center points. The design was intended to characterize linear, interaction, and quadratic effects, while the axial distance was selected to avoid undesirable vertices of the parameter hypercube and simplify the feasible region. For operational consistency, all samples belonging to one active-learning iteration were printed in a single batch. This reduced iterative time and cost and limited between-batch variation. A fixed 30 μm layer thickness was used so that samples in each iteration could be printed together. Center points were repeated across batches and analyzed with a fixed-effect one-way ANOVA to test whether batch significantly affected relative density. This is explicitly acknowledged as a simplified batch-consistency assessment because it samples only the center of the design space and treats batch as fixed rather than random. Measurements were also temporally randomized. Gaussian-process regression with uncertainty estimates is proposed as the surrogate framework supporting active learning, but the excerpt does not identify the acquisition function or quantify the number of builds required.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization and active-learning strategy for LPBF process-window modeling. The surrogate combines a computationally inexpensive low-fidelity thermal solver with a high-fidelity, full-resolution heat-conduction simulation using an autoregressive multi-fidelity Gaussian process. High-fidelity sampling is acquisition-driven: the upper confidence bound (UCB), defined as the posterior mean plus an exploration-weighted standard deviation, selects points by maximizing the criterion. This balances exploitation near promising process settings with exploration of uncertain regions. Low-fidelity sampling is intended primarily to improve global surrogate accuracy and is selected by maximizing the low-fidelity predictive standard deviation, thereby targeting unexplored regions and increasing information gain. The procedure uses a fixed high-to-low fidelity sampling ratio, r = m/n, where m is the number of low-fidelity evaluations per iteration and n is typically one high-fidelity evaluation. The ratio is predetermined and constant, supporting consistent updates and budget planning. The excerpt does not specify actual experimental batch sizes, numbers of physical LPBF builds, replicate counts, hold-out points, or a separate experimental-design protocol. It concerns simulation-based fidelity allocation, although the framework could inform such decisions.

contexts.context: The excerpt gives empirical stability thresholds for the Keyhole number Ke in laser powder bed fusion. For Ke<16, keyhole fluctuations are small, porosity is nearly absent, and spattering is rare. For Ke>30, the keyhole becomes chaotic and unstable; small perturbations can produce large wall fluctuations, leading to pore and spatter formation. contexts.context: Gan et al. define the dimensionless Keyhole number as Ke = P*/(Pe T*), where P* is normalized laser power, Pe is the Peclet number, and T* is normalized temperature. In expanded physical terms, Ke combines the effective laser energy density, the inverse sensible heat required for vaporization, and a dimensionless factor representing the relative separation of vaporization and melting isotherms. The authors report that normalized keyhole depth collapses onto a universal curve when plotted against Ke, despite variations in laser power, scan speed, spot size, and material. Their parsimonious keyhole-depth relation is e* = 5.12 − 5.07 exp[−1.0 P*/(Pe T*)], equivalently expressed using Ke. The excerpt does not provide a numerical threshold for keyhole stability; it only states that the exponential scaling is expected to become linear once Ke exceeds a threshold at which absorptivity approaches one. For porosity, the paper uses a separate five-variable dimensional representation and gives a genetic-programming model involving normalized melting and vaporization energy-density groupings, Peclet number, hatch spacing, and temperature. Thus, Ke is presented as a universal keyhole-depth criterion, while porosity prediction is modeled separately rather than through Ke alone.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides a general framework for Bayesian optimization in additive manufacturing experimental design, but it does not specify recommended batch sizes, the number of LPBF builds, the number of experiments required, replicate counts, hold-out validation procedures, or whether Latin hypercube or Sobol designs should be used. It states that additive manufacturing has an enlarged design space and therefore benefits from a structured, systematic search. The basic BO loop uses a surrogate model—here, a Gaussian process—to represent the black-box objective and an acquisition function to select the next experiment. At each iteration, a candidate is selected by optimizing the acquisition function, evaluated experimentally, added to the dataset, and used to update the surrogate. An identifiability problem was found: correlations among the three parameters created a continuous range of similarly likely posterior values constrained mainly by parameter bounds. A Gaussian process regression (GPR) emulator is trained from an initial Latin hypercube sample and then refined through active learning. contexts.context: The excerpt focuses primarily on lack-of-fusion (LOF) and spatter-related porosity in 316L stainless steel, rather than providing a complete assessment of keyhole modeling or overall defect-prediction accuracy. It shows that a constant volumetric energy density can produce substantially different melt-pool geometries and defect types, indicating that VED alone is an inadequate predictor. LOF in Cubes 1 and 7 was associated with insufficient overlap between melt pools, while defects in Cubes 3, 6, and 9 formed within melt pools and were attributed mainly to spatter or particles driven by high laser shock pressure. Cube 6 may contain both spatter-induced LOF and a spherical gas pore. The authors argue that conventional LOF criteria based on Rosenthal-model semicircular melt pools are limited because experimentally observed pools are generally non-semicircular, with width-to-depth ratios changing as laser power and scanning velocity vary. They propose modifying the criteria by representing the melt pool as a semi-ellipse with a variable aspect ratio calibrated to experiments, while preserving approximately constant melt-pool volume. The excerpt does not mention the Concept Laser M2 platform, provide quantitative model accuracy, or discuss keyhole criteria in detail.

contexts.context: The excerpt evaluates volumetric energy density (VED) as a predictor of defects in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) 316L stainless steel. Nine parameter sets varied laser power, scanning velocity, and hatch spacing while maintaining the same VED. Despite identical VED values, the specimens showed systematic differences in both pore type and pore amount, indicating that VED alone is only correlational and cannot represent the distinct mechanisms producing defects. The article considers keyhole porosity, lack-of-fusion (LOF) porosity, and spatter-related defects. Keyholing occurs when the laser sufficiently vaporizes material, potentially creating cavities, while LOF results from inadequate remelting or overlap between melt pools and layers. Spatter, often associated with high laser power, can land on solidifying material and generate intrapass LOF; the excerpt notes that no analytical model previously predicted when spatter or powder ejection would occur. The authors use analytical defect maps and propose a modified interpass LOF criterion plus a new spatter-induced intrapass LOF criterion, intended to improve predictions at low-power/low-speed and high-power/high-speed conditions, respectively. This excerpt does not provide numerical accuracy results or identify whether the experiments used a Concept Laser M2 system.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Smith et al.’s comparison of constant volumetric energy density with analytical defect maps for predicting porosity in laser powder bed fusion of 316L stainless steel. The study examines keyhole, lack-of-fusion (LOF), and gas-porosity mechanisms. Lack of fusion is associated with insufficient melting and may occur when spatter or powder ejection contributes to incomplete fusion within melt pools. Keyholing is linked to excessive heat input: laser heating can generate vapor or plasma, producing a cavity that may collapse or remain as a pore after solidification. However, keyhole formation does not necessarily mean retained porosity. The analytical keyhole criterion is based on Hann’s normalized-enthalpy concept, in which keyholing becomes more likely when normalized enthalpy exceeds a boiling-temperature-to-melting-temperature ratio. Defect maps use analytical expressions to identify laser-power and scanning-speed combinations that avoid keyhole and LOF porosity for fixed layer thickness and hatch spacing. Experimentally, builds were made on a 3D Systems DMP Flex 350—not a Concept Laser M2—with multiple laser powers, scanning speeds, and hatch spacings held at 85 J/mm³. contexts.context: Smith et al. evaluated analytical defect-map models for keyhole porosity, lack-of-fusion (LOF), and newly proposed spatter-induced porosity in laser powder bed fusion of 316L stainless steel. Nine parameter combinations were examined, varying laser power, scan velocity, and hatch spacing while maintaining the same volumetric energy density. The results show that volumetric energy density alone does not reliably predict either porosity type or porosity amount: substantially different levels of LOF, gas, and spatter-induced porosity occurred at constant volumetric energy density. The study also emphasizes that defect formation depends on the combined effects of laser power, velocity, layer height, hatch spacing, and preheat temperature. Interpass LOF caused by insufficient melt-track overlap occurred at low laser powers and scan speeds and was not captured well by conventional LOF criteria based on semicircular melt-pool assumptions. A modified LOF criterion incorporating actual melt-pool width and depth geometry better predicted this porosity. At higher laser powers and scan speeds, intrapass spatter-induced LOF was associated with increased laser shock pressure. The authors conclude that defect maps organized by individual defect mechanisms provide more accurate process guidance than volumetric-energy-density relationships. The excerpt does not identify the machine as a Concept Laser M2.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents analytical defect-threshold models for laser powder bed fusion, but it does not specifically discuss Smith 316L, the Concept Laser M2 machine, volumetric energy density experiments, spatter, modified criteria, or prediction accuracy. Lack of fusion is modeled using a geometric molten-pool criterion: H²/W² + L²/D² ≤ 1, where H is hatch spacing, L is layer thickness, and W and D are molten-pool width and depth; lack of fusion is predicted when this condition is not satisfied. Balling is associated with low energy density and poor molten-pool wettability, with a criterion based on πw/l > 1, where w and l are molten-pool width and length. Keyholing is linked to material evaporation and is predicted through normalized enthalpy relationships involving laser power, scanning speed, absorptivity, beam diameter, melting and boiling temperatures, thermal diffusivity, and specific heat. The article also calculates temperature fields by superposing laser heating and convection/radiation heat-loss solutions, while accounting for powder-bed porosity and its effect on thermal conductivity. Thus, this passage provides baseline analytical criteria that could be compared with modified volumetric-energy-density models, but it contains no machine-specific validation or quantitative accuracy results.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides results primarily for the NiTi validation case. Because NiTi was highly sensitive to processing parameters, the authors initially generated a printability map using grid sampling and then printed 60 single tracks to revise it. Experimental melt-pool measurements were used to calibrate the analytical E-T thermal model. The calibrated model produced a revised printability map identifying three keyholing boundaries, one lack-of-fusion boundary, and one balling boundary. A keyholing threshold of W/D ≤ 2 was selected because it yielded the lowest misclassification for the characterized tracks, and maximum hatch-spacing contours were overlaid to finalize the map. Eight parameter combinations were used to fabricate density coupons; five exceeded 99% density, and four combinations above 99.9% density were selected for tensile specimens. Their ultimate tensile strengths ranged from 454 to 623 MPa, with elongations of 8.6–9.7%. The broader framework integrates an analytical thermal model, single-track experiments, and uncertainty quantification to identify processing regimes and low-porosity parameter windows. The excerpt specifically details NiNb5 (approximately 5.08 wt% Nb), produced by gas atomization, with a powder d80 of 30 µm used as the layer thickness. Single-track experiments were used to revise and finalize a printability map, with regions classified according to defects including keyholing, lack of fusion, and balling; white regions denote good printability. Maximum hatch-spacing contours were added to the finalized map. Bulk coupons were subsequently selected from the map, with density/porosity assessed through optical microscopy and ImageJ analysis. Mechanical specimens were cut from printed blocks by wire EDM and tensile-tested at room temperature at a strain rate of 5 × 10^-4 s^-1.
